Pressing "Hard To Rattle" is layer 4 — the personality trait's own body: what you gave up to take it, and every knob it currently moves, each of which is a Look back into a wellbeing dial. That is a cycle in the graph, which is fine: the path is a tree even when the subject graph is not, and exclusive siblings keep the page bounded. WHAT THE PLAYER SEES WHILE ALL THIS IS OPEN. The sticky strip at the top of the page reads `You › How You Are › Stress › Why You Shed It Faster`. The panel below has grown by roughly 260px. Energy and Readiness have not moved relative to each other. `Where You Are` and `Money` have been pushed down the page but are unchanged, and the right-hand column has not moved at all. Escape collapses one level and puts the trail back to `You › How You Are › Stress`. Pressing "Stress" again closes the whole branch, and `.main` scrolls back so the meter is where it was. TWO THINGS THAT ARE NOW TRUE AND WERE NOT. `wellbeing.stress` is registered once, so the same Look opens from the Sleep dialog's suggestion reason and from a future notification, identically. And the four dials that reach no screen today — sleepDebt, morale, travelFatigue, hygiene — are registered kinds reachable from Readiness's body, which is the only way a player would ever learn they exist.
designs.costs:
WHERE THIS ANGLE IS GENUINELY WEAK, in order of how much it would hurt.

1. IT DESYNCS A TWO-COLUMN GRID, AND HOME IS ONE. `How You Are` sits in `.grid-2` beside `What Needs You` (Home.tsx:110). A depth-3 expansion in the left column adds 600px to that column and nothing to the right one, which then floats with a half-screen of dead space beside it. The clean fix — break the body out to `grid-column: 1 / -1` — is impossible, because the Look is nested three levels inside the left card and cannot escape its container without a portal, which is the thing this angle exists to avoid. Below 900px the grid is one column and the problem vanishes entirely; above it, the honest answer is that deep drilling on Home leaves an empty right column. A modal-stack design has no equivalent failure. If this angle is chosen, panels that are expected to go deep should be laid out full-width, which is a real constraint on future screen design.

2. A DEEP LOOK MAKES THE PAGE VERY LONG. Even with exclusive siblings, four bodies of prose plus stats is perhaps 1,200px inserted mid-page. Everything below it is a screenful away, and on a phone the surrounding page effectively stops existing — you are scrolling a column of text, which is not obviously better than the modal it replaced. Exclusive siblings and the sticky trail keep it navigable; they do not keep it short.

3. NO LINK, NO URL, NO SHARE, NO REFRESH. Open state is a `Set<string>` in provider state and `sessionStorage`. It survives navigate() and it survives switching screens and coming back, which is more than any deleted precedent managed. It does not survive reload, cannot be linked, and cannot be reopened from a notification's `refType/refId` at a specific depth without extra work. The paths are designed to be serialisable so this is later work rather than foreclosed work, but it is not in the first version.

4. YOU CANNOT PUT TWO DISTANT THINGS SIDE BY SIDE. A calendar entry and the entry it clashes with are two rows apart on one screen, so that case works. A calendar entry and the person it is about are not, and in-place expansion can never show them together — you would have to open one inside the other, which nests rather than compares. `LookGroup compare` only helps siblings. A master-detail split or a modal handles this; in-place does not.

5. NO HEIGHT ANIMATION, SO IT IS SLIGHTLY ABRUPT. Animating the height of a growing nested tree is expensive and lands badly at depth 3. I would ship the scroll anchoring animated and the expansion itself instant. It reads as sharp rather than smooth, and a modal fade genuinely feels more considered.

WHAT IT FORECLOSES, DELIBERATELY.

Depth in the same viewport can never be a focus mode. A body that wants the whole screen — the 813-attribute sheet, the estate as a map, a full account statement — must become a route with a named control leading to it, which means the architecture ends up with two depth systems: Looks for looking, routes for staying. I think that split is correct, but it is a split, and it will need policing so that the second one does not slowly swallow the first.

It also forecloses the nested-modal stack for read-only depth, which means the four TimeControls dialogs and their inert lists cannot use it — a Look inside a Modal would expand inside the modal's own scroller, which is the one place where "pushing the page down" is actually cramped. Those lists get Looks anyway; they will just be a little tight.

FILES THIS TOUCHES THAT ARE ALREADY LOAD-BEARING. `primitives.tsx` (Stat and Meter change shape; `hint` is deleted, and its one call site at Home.tsx:202 must move), `game-context.tsx` (three new context fields and a hotkey guard), `GameShell.tsx` (LookRoot mounts around `.main-inner`), and `app.css`'s `.sheet` rules, whose `content: 'Show'` / `'Hide'` toggle words are a STYLE.md violation living where no gate can read them and should be replaced by a Look opener at the same time.

ranking: Design 2 — The Long Look (persistent inspector column)
Design 1 — The Trail (address carried in the route)
Design 3 — The Drill Stack (portalled cascade of sheets)
verdicts.why:
Judged on immersion alone, one distinction sorts all four: is the drill affordance a WORD IN A SENTENCE, or a ROW WITH A CONTROL ON IT? Only Design 4 is the former, and that is the whole ballgame. A settings tree is made of rows with controls; prose is made of words. Design 4's opener is `button.link` — which app.css:328 already defines, already comments as "A name that is also a way in", and has never once used. The stylesheet wrote this feature's core affordance and then waited for someone to notice. Its worked example ("Stress only goes on when you're *running on empty*, and you haven't been") puts the two drills inside a spoken clause. The other three all hang depth off a Stat label, a Meter label or a `.list-item` — record furniture — and therefore read as a schema browser with good typography no matter how well the bodies are written.

Second: Design 4 is the only one where nothing is ever covered and nothing is ever "gone to". Pressing the word opens the world underneath it; pressing it again closes it. There is no Back button, because the thing you pressed is still on screen and is still the way out. Compare what the lens is ruthless about. Design 3 is the worst offender by a distance: a portalled cascade over a dimmed backdrop, focus traps, `inert` ancestors, scroll lock, Escape popping levels, and a 26px ancestor strip whose accessible name is literally "Back To Stress" — a back button in a costume, plus a trail in every sheet header. "Layered glass" is an interface metaphor; there is no glass in Reykjavik. Its content rules are the best in the set and its engineering is the most honest, but the shape it produces says "you have opened a dialog chain over the game."

Design 1 commits the specific sin the lens names first. It renders looking at your own stress as `Home › You › How You Are › Stress › Highly Strung` in the same breadcrumb bar used for moving between screens, so the visible consequence of examining a number is a navigation path appearing and growing. It teaches the player that their own body has an address — and that address (`person:person_000001/wellbeing/dial:stress`) reaches `favourites`, which is localStorage the player owns, and which the design concedes can end up pointing at a lens that no longer exists. Design 2 is right in its own text that merging "which screen am I on" with "what am I looking at" is what makes a breadcrumb read as a file path, and Design 1 does exactly that by construction. Its virtues are real — the parent stays lit, `title()` is separate from `kind`, `gone` is required — but its central move is "depth is navigation," and the lens wants "depth is reading."

Design 2 places third-from-bottom on one word: furniture. A permanent inspector column is the literal shape of a database browser; the name is not an accident. Its empty state is an instruction manual living on screen at all times ("Press anything to look at it closer"), and the design admits an empty column is a weaker opening state than nothing at all. It never darkens the world, which is genuinely the best structural immersion argument any of the four makes, and its content contract is the strongest in the set — but a place in the interface that is always there whether or not you asked is a tool, and 232px of rail plus 360px of inspector is 592px of permanent chrome taxing the only two screens that exist. Ranked above Design 1 anyway, because constant chrome is less corrosive than chrome that grows every time you look closer.

Phones confirm the order rather than complicating it. Design 2 degrades to a 65% bottom sheet (a modal wearing a name, by its own admission), Design 1 to a full-width sheet, Design 3's ancestor strips vanish entirely so its whole argument dies. Design 4 gets BETTER: below 900px the grid is one column and in-place expansion is simply how reading works. The design whose central claim survives the small screen is the one whose central claim was about the world rather than about the layout.

The one thing Design 4 must be honest about: the grid desync is real and unfixable from inside the angle. `How You Are` sits in `.grid-2` beside `What Needs You` (Home.tsx:110); a depth-3 expansion adds ~600px to the left column and nothing to the right, and the Look is nested too deep to escape its container without the portal this design exists to avoid. Above 900px, deep drilling leaves a half-empty right column, which reads as a broken screen — an immersion cost paid in layout rather than in voice. The mitigation is a permanent constraint on future screen design: panels expected to go deep get laid out full-width. That is a real price and worth paying for an affordance that is a word rather than a widget.
graft: FACET TABS, from Design 2 — the single most valuable idea in the losing three, and the one Design 4 needs most. A person is not Person › Wellbeing › Stress and Person › Money and Person › Standing as three descents; it is one body with lateral tabs (How You Are · Standing · The Work · Where You've Been) using `.tabs`/`.tab`, fully written at app.css:749-762 and rendered nowhere. This attacks Design 4's worst cost head-on: in-place expansion punishes depth with page length, and facets collapse most of the intended 4- and 5-layer chains into two levels plus a tab row. Carry the rule verbatim: a tab is a facet of the SAME thing, a Look is a DIFFERENT thing.

REQUIRED `summary`, from Design 2. Design 4's registry has `summary?` optional; make it mandatory and second person. A view with only numbers to offer then has to write the sentence anyway, and that pressure is the only thing that reliably stops a body from becoming a record dump. `wellbeingSummary` (life.ts:96-105) is the proven shape — seven floats into 'Badly short on sleep. Everything is harder than it should be.'

THE NAME GATE, from Design 2 — a test walking `lookKinds()` that fails any `name()` output containing `_`, `/`, a digit-run of four or more, or any registered kind string. 'Sleep Debt' passes; 'sleepDebt', 'Atlantic/Reykjavik', 'Shootday' and 'person_000001' cannot ship. Highest immersion leverage per line in the whole sweep, and it is what structurally prevents `labelForRoute`'s slug-prettifier (game-context.tsx:308-312) from ever producing 'Is 39 Reykjavik'.

`kind` SEPARATE FROM `name`, AND A REQUIRED HAND-WRITTEN `gone`, from Design 1. Design 4's `LookView` has `name` but no eyebrow and no dead-address sentence. Split them so the type word has an honest home above the title and never enters it — the reason `Modal`'s `title: string` produces headings like 'Calendar Entry'. And every kind writes its own `gone` in the world's voice ('That's not one of yours any more'), so a stale ref never lands on WorkspaceRouter.tsx:14's 'That workspace doesn't exist' or world.ts:37's 'No such decision.'

`Open` REFUSES TO PAINT WHEN NOTHING RESOLVES, from Design 2 — renders children as plain text rather than a dead control. Design 4 throws in dev and degrades in production; take the runtime version instead. This is `.cal-event { cursor: pointer }` on spans with no handler (app.css:787) made structurally impossible, and it is the real answer to the Locked-toast pattern at GameShell.tsx:46-49: a drill that would end in Under Construction is simply not painted as a drill.

WAYS CARRY THEIR CONSEQUENCE, from Design 2 — every way in is a name plus a line saying what is behind it, in the `.menu-item-label` + `.menu-item-detail` shape TimeControls already proved reads well (app.css:1143-1144). 'What Sheds It — the hourly recovery, and what's multiplying it.' Being able to read the graph without walking it is the strongest anti-corridor device after facets, and it costs nothing in a design whose bodies are prose already.

ONE VIEW, TWO CONTAINERS, from Design 2. Design 4 says a body wanting the whole screen 'becomes a route'; Design 2's version is strictly better — the SAME registered view renders full-width at `/look/:kind/:id`. One authoring surface, not two, so the 813-attribute sheet and a year of daylight do not fork into a second implementation the gates measure separately.

MATERIALISED INTERMEDIATE DEPTH FOR DEEP LINKS, from Design 1. Design 4 files this as later work; it should not be. A notification carrying `refType/refId` that opens only the leaf is the most disorienting case in the feature. Walking the serialisable path and opening the whole chain — so one press from a notification lands with `You › How You Are › Stress` already open above it — is the thing that stops depth 4 with one crumb.

DO NOT PERSIST DEPTH INTO THE SAVE, from Design 1, adopted explicitly rather than by omission. sessionStorage yes, `SaveUniverse` no. The world moves while you are away; resuming four levels inside a number you were looking at last Tuesday is stranger than landing on Home, and it buys a `validateUniverse` surface for nothing.

MODAL COMMITS, A LOOK ONLY READS — and portal `Modal` regardless, from Design 3. I confirmed the bug: `.topbar` is `position: relative; z-index: 20` (app.css:587) and establishes a stacking context, so the three TimeControls dialogs' `.overlay` at z-index 200 (app.css:767) is capped at 20 and renders UNDER the mobile rail drawer at 30 (app.css:637) and its shade at 29 (:694). Design 4 does not need the portal for itself, which is exactly why it will otherwise leave this unfixed forever.

ESCAPE OWNERSHIP AT CAPTURE PHASE, from Design 3. Design 4's `document.querySelector('[role="dialog"]')` guard is a DOM sniff; a capture-phase `window` listener with `stopImmediatePropagation` is the actual mechanism, and it is the only thing that stops one Escape from closing a Look, the rail drawer (GameShell.tsx:38-43) and a Modal (primitives.tsx:126-130) simultaneously. Swallow bare `h`/`c` at depth > 0 in the same listener — game-context.tsx:268-279 guards only INPUT/TEXTAREA/SELECT, so today they change the screen underneath an open dialog.

`redactForPlayer` AS THE TERMINUS FOR EVERY 'WHY', from Design 3. `core/audit.ts` has it and a per-factor `knowable` flag, fully written, zero callers. Any body answering why routes through it rather than growing a second explanation system. This is the concrete guarantee behind both designs' shared rule that no formula is ever a level — the mechanism that keeps looking closer from becoming opening the debugger.

'NARROWING A SET IS A FILTER INSIDE ONE LEVEL, NOT A NEW LEVEL', from Design 3, taken verbatim as a review rule. Without it, in-place expansion grows a body per list click and the sticky trail turns into a click log inside a month. A new level means a DIFFERENT OBJECT.

ENUMERABILITY AND GATE COVERAGE, from Designs 2 and 3 together. `lookKinds()` must let `tools/cohesion-walk.mjs` open every body and `tools/text-caps.mjs` measure every one at its five widths — a layer no tool can enumerate is a layer no tool can see. And extend `label-sweep.mjs` (engine-only today) and `voice-check.mjs` to `src/ui/looks/**` in the same commit, or the feature ships a hundred unpoliced strings into the one directory where all the new prose lives.
verdicts.fatal:
None of the four is unworkable; all four are buildable as specified. Three honest qualifications, in descending order of how much they should change the decision.

(1) Design 4's grid desync is the only defect in the set that cannot be repaired from inside its own design. A Look nested three levels into the left card of Home's `.grid-2` (Home.tsx:110) cannot break out to `grid-column: 1 / -1` without a portal, and the portal is the exact thing the angle exists to refuse. Above 900px, deep drilling therefore leaves a half-screen of dead space in the right column. It is not fatal — below 900px the grid is one column and the problem disappears entirely, and the fix above 900px is a layout convention (panels expected to go deep are laid out full-width) rather than a code change. But it is a permanent constraint on every screen SLATE has not built yet, and it should be accepted with open eyes rather than discovered at depth 3.

(2) Two designs make a central immersion claim that they themselves concede evaporates on a phone. Design 2's entire case is "the world never goes dark," which below ~1024px becomes a 65% bottom sheet — the design's own text calls this "a modal wearing a different name." Design 3's case is the visible ancestor strips, which below 700px go to zero offset and vanish, at which point the cascade covers the world exactly as a modal does and the trail is carrying the whole load alone. Neither is unworkable; both are arguments that hold only on a laptop, and both authors say so plainly, which is to their credit and is also the reason neither wins.

(3) Design 1 introduces a real defect on day one and correctly flags it: `GameShell.tsx:190` (`route === '/home'`, `route.startsWith('/workspace/')`), `WorkspaceRouter.tsx:8` (`WORKSPACES[route]`) and the rail's `aria-current={route === item.route}` all compare the raw route, so `/workspace/calendar?look=…` passes `startsWith`, misses the map, and renders "Nothing Here Yet" while the rail stops marking the current screen — which `tools/cohesion-walk.mjs` fails on by name ("a rail that marks the wrong screen"). This is a one-function fix shipped in the same commit, not a fatal flaw, but it is worth noting that the design's mechanism requires breaking three existing comparisons to work at all.

What I would flag as close to fatal in spirit rather than in engineering: Design 3's ancestor strip with the accessible name "Back To Stress". Under this lens specifically, building a back button, styling it as a sliver of the thing behind, and giving it a spoken name that begins with the word "Back" is the design admitting it produced navigation and then dressing it. Everything else about Design 3 — the eyebrow/name split, no-formula-is-ever-a-level, `redactForPlayer` as terminus, capture-phase Escape — is first-rate and should survive into the winner. The container it puts them in is the problem.

verdicts.why:
DEPTH LENS: I tested each against two chains that genuinely exist in the engine. Chain A: Home → How You Are (9 dials, six of which reach no screen) → Stress → What Sheds It (`recovery = modifierFor(person,'recoveryRate') × personalityOf(person,'stressRecovery')`, life.ts:78, where `dispositionOf` = `traitModifier × axisModifier`, taste.ts:110-140) → Highly Strung (`systemMods: { stressGain: 1.35, sleepQuality: 0.88, moraleSwing: 1.25 }`, personality-traits.ts:61) → Sleep Quality, which is another dial. That chain is 5-6 deep, has real content at every level, and is CYCLIC. Chain B: Home → Reykjavík → Iceland → Income Tax → the rule (`resolveIncomeTaxLayers`, tax.ts:322) → a bracket (`TaxBracket`, tax.ts:19). Also 5-6 deep, all real data.

WHAT SEPARATES THEM AT LAYER 4. Designs 1, 2 and 3 all hold depth as one array, re-resolve addresses against `sim`, and put a full trail in front of the player, so all three answer "does depth 5 cost what depth 2 costs" with yes. The tiebreaker is what layer 4 knows about itself.

Design 1 is the only one whose trail is DERIVED FROM THE ADDRESS rather than from click history. `resolvePath` materialises every intermediate crumb by walking the segments, so a player who lands at depth 4 in one press — a meter on Home, a notification's `refType/refId`, a restored favourite — arrives with `Home › You › How You Are › Stress › Highly Strung` fully populated. In Designs 2 and 3 the trail is a push-stack: `jump()` / a ref-resolve deposits you at layer 4 with a one-item trail and no ancestry, and that is precisely the layer-4 failure mode the requirement is about. In Design 4 you cannot land deep at all — a nested `<Look>` only renders inside its parent's `Body`, so depth is reachable only from wherever a screen already paints the root noun.

Design 1 also handles the cyclic graph correctly and the others do not, or do so awkwardly. Its resolution is relative-then-absolute, so `.../dial:stress/trait:highly_strung/dial:sleep-quality` is an honest walk that crosses from a number to a thing to another number, and the crumb reads as a sentence. Design 4 has to declare "the path is a tree even when the subject graph is not" and then render a wellbeing dial six levels of DOM deep inside the card it started in.

And the shell already implements the two gestures depth needs: `navigate` push-with-truncate and crumb-click-to-ancestor (game-context.tsx:161-180) plus the rendered trail (GameShell.tsx:155-169). Putting the path in the route means depth-5 navigation is code that already exists and is already tested, rather than a second parallel stack.

WHY NOT 2. The Long Look has the best single layer-4 device of any of the four — the parent line, printing the parent's name AND its one-sentence summary above the current level, so layer 4 always shows layer 3's point. That is better context than a stack gets from the pane behind it. It also has the strongest anti-corridor device (facets as a typed field, `Facet[]`, so a facet structurally cannot become a level). But it caps detail at 360px and then needs a whole second container (`/look/:type/:id`) for exactly the layers that got detailed enough to need room — the tax bracket table, the trait's modifier list. Under a lens that asks for INCREASINGLY DETAILED sub-systems, a fixed-width column that gets no wider as the content gets denser is the wrong shape, and its own worked example concedes the escape hatch. Its trail is also click history, so ref-entry lands shallow.

WHY NOT 3. The Drill Stack gives layer 5 the most room (560px), owns Escape properly at capture phase — which is the only real answer to the verified fact that `Modal` (primitives.tsx:126-130), the rail drawer (GameShell.tsx:38-43) and the Advance menu all register bubble-phase `window` keydowns — and offers four exits that all work at depth 5. But it ships NO lateral device at all. Its only defence against manufactured depth is the review rule "narrowing a set is a filter, not a level," which its own costs section admits will turn the trail into a click log within a month. A person's Craft / Standing / Money / History become four descents instead of one level with tabs, and then a nominal depth 5 is really depth 2 plus three clicks. It also drops `navigate()` on the stack, so you cannot carry a drill across screens.

WHY 4 IS LAST AND CAPS OUT AT TWO. This is the design the lens exists to catch. Three verified reasons, in order:

(1) WIDTH SHRINKS AS DEPTH GROWS. Layer 4 is nested inside layer 3 inside layer 2 inside a `.card` inside a `grid-2` cell inside `.main-inner` (1180px, minus the 232px rail). Layer 4 has materially LESS horizontal room than layer 1, minus two `--surface` insets and a 2px rule per level. Every other design gives layer 4 the same width as layer 1. A design where detail increases while the container contracts is the definitional opposite of the requirement.

(2) THE LAYOUT FAILURE IS REAL AND ADMITTED. `.grid-2` is `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(260px,100%),1fr))` (app.css:347) and `How You Are` is in the right cell of Home's grid-2 (Home.tsx:110). A depth-4 expansion adds ~1,200px to one cell and nothing to its sibling, and the design correctly says the clean fix — `grid-column: 1 / -1` — is impossible without the portal it exists to avoid. So on the only screen that ships, deep drilling produces a half-screen of dead column. That is not a cost; that is the design failing at exactly the depth being asked for.

(3) EXCLUSIVE SIBLINGS ARE A DEPTH TAX. The rule that bounds the page also forbids holding two facts of one level open at once, so at layer 4 you cannot see Stress's gain flow and shed flow together — the comparison the other three make trivially.

Add: it fails inside a Modal (a Look expands into the modal's own scroller), it cannot be deep-linked, and at layer 4 the opener you would press to close is 1,200px up the page, leaving a 28px sticky strip as the only usable exit.

Design 4 is genuinely the best design in this set at LAYER ONE and LAYER TWO. Nothing is covered, the parent stays lit, and `button.link` — already written in the stylesheet and commented "A name that is also a way in" (app.css:328) and used nowhere — is the correct affordance for a noun in prose. It is the wrong engine and the right primitive, which is why grafts 6 and 7 below take it wholesale rather than discarding it.

ONE BUG IN THE WINNER THAT ITS OWN WRITE-UP GETS WRONG, and it is a depth bug. Design 1 claims "`back()` IS pop-one-level ... it is game-context.tsx:172-180 unchanged." That is false. `back()` pops one BREADCRUMB, and `navigate` pushes exactly one crumb per call. If crumbs are materialised by `resolvePath` (which is the design's own headline depth property), the crumb array is no longer the depth stack, and a one-press deep link to depth 3 pushes ONE crumb — so `back()` discards all three levels at once instead of popping one. `closeLook()` must own popping one look segment, and `back()` must delegate to it whenever the route carries a `?look=`. This is correctable and is already half-present in the proposed API, but it must be built, not inherited.
graft: From Design 2 — THE PARENT LINE. This is the single most valuable idea in the losing three and the winner has nothing like it. A rail renders only the tip of the trail, so at layer 4 the crumb 'Stress' is a name with no state attached. Print the parent lens's `title()` plus its one-sentence summary in dim text above the current level's name, so layer 4 always carries layer 3's point. Cheap, and better context than a stacked pane's visible edge.

From Design 2 — FACETS AS A TYPED FIELD, NOT A REVIEW RULE. Design 1 states the tabs rule in prose ('facets of one object are tabs inside a level'), which is exactly the discipline Design 3 admits will slip. Move it into the type: add `facets?: { id, label, body, children? }[]` to `Lens` and render `.tabs`/`.tab`, which is fully styled at app.css:749-762 and used nowhere. A facet that cannot be addressed cannot become a level. This is the load-bearing anti-corridor device and it must be structural.

From Design 3 — SHEET WIDTH AND FULL-WIDTH PROMOTION. Do NOT render the trail tip in `.side-by-side`'s sidebar; that track is `minmax(220px, 320px)` (app.css:467), narrower than the column Design 2 already concedes is too tight for a 9-bracket tax table or a trait's modifier list. Take Design 3's ~560px. And take the promotion idea, which the winner gets nearly free and never claims: because a Design 1 address IS a route, `/look?look=<same address>` renders the same lens full-width in `.main` with zero new addressing machinery. One lens, two containers, no second address scheme — which is strictly better than Design 2's bolted-on `/look/:type/:id`.

From Design 3 — CAPTURE-PHASE ESCAPE OWNERSHIP. Design 1 claims it sidesteps the Escape fight by not being a modal. It does not: `Modal` still registers a bubble-phase `window` keydown per instance (primitives.tsx:126-130) and so does the rail drawer (GameShell.tsx:38-43). With a lens open at depth 4, Escape must pop exactly one look segment and nothing else. Register on `window` at capture with `stopImmediatePropagation()`. Same listener should swallow bare `h`/`c` while depth > 0 — today they change the screen underneath an open dialog (game-context.tsx:268-279 guards only INPUT/TEXTAREA/SELECT).

From Design 3 — MACHINE-ENUMERABLE DEPTH. Export the registry enumeration and crawl `children()` transitively so `tools/walkthrough.mjs` can open every layer and `tools/ui-audit.mjs` can measure every layer at four widths. Without this, layers 3-5 are never opened by a tool and rot silently — which is the specific way a depth engine dies. Design 1's `children()` field already makes the crawl possible; it just has to be wired to the tools and to a test asserting every declared child address resolves against a fresh save.

From Design 4 — THE NOUN IS THE CONTROL, IN PROSE. Design 1's `open` props on `Stat`/`Meter`/`Row` cover grids and lists but leave prose inert, and a level made only of openable cells is the stat-grid failure mode it says it wants to avoid. Take Design 4's in-sentence opener wholesale: a `button.link` carrying the world's own words ('running on empty', 'faster for you than for most people'), using the class already written and unused at app.css:328. This is what turns layer 3 from a table of drivers into a sentence you can press, and it is the mechanism by which the winner's 'prose first, facts second' contract is actually reachable.

From Design 4 and Design 3 — RESERVE THE TRAIL FOR CROSSING TO A DIFFERENT OBJECT. Level 1 of something that is part of what you are already reading stays a `<details>`/`.sheet` in place; the trail starts when you cross to a different object. Both losers independently reached this rule and it is the one that keeps a 5-deep trail readable as a sentence rather than a click log. Pair it with Design 4's exclusive-sibling discipline for those in-place reveals so the page cannot grow unbounded.

From Design 2 — MAKE THE OPENING SENTENCE A REQUIRED FIELD. Design 1 has `title`, `eyebrow` and `gone` but leaves prose-first as a render convention, and a convention will not survive forty lenses. Add a required `summary(sim, subject): string` so a layer physically cannot ship as a grid of Stats. `wellbeingSummary` (life.ts:96-105) is the existing proof of the register.

## Verdict: broken. Readiness has no layer-2 object, and the design's own rules forbid all three ways of inventing one.

### The facts

`readiness()` is `src/engine/systems/life.ts:82-95`. It is a pure function of `person.wellbeing`, called in exactly one place in the repo — `src/ui/screens/Home.tsx:39`, to paint `Home.tsx:202`. Nothing in the engine consumes it. It is not a field: `Wellbeing` (`src/engine/domain/model.ts:32-54`) has nine keys and `readiness` is not among them. Its body is:

```ts
return clamp(100 * energyPart * stressPart * debtPart * nourishPart
             * moralePart * travelPart * cleanPart / 1.35, 5, 100);
```

Seven `remap` calls multiplied together and divided by a magic 1.35.

### Failure 1 — the address scheme cannot name it

`Subject = {kind, id}` addresses two things in practice: record ids (`entry:…`) and **struct paths** (`dial:person_000001/stress` is `person.wellbeing.stress`). Readiness is neither. It is a *call*. `at('dial', 'person_000001/readiness')` sends the dial view's `resolve` to a key that does not exist, it returns `undefined`, and rule 3 + `gone` make the design print "it is no longer there" about a number that is on screen, has never been absent, and cannot be. That is the worst possible failure mode for a system whose whole pitch is immersion.

And the mechanism's headline argument — `subjectForRef` unifying `refType`/`refId` across `CalendarEntry`, `DecisionItem`, `Notification`, `ScheduledItem`, `LedgerTransaction`, `HistoryRecord.refs` — buys **zero** here. Every one of those addresses a persisted record. Readiness has no record and never will.

### Failure 2 — minting `kind: 'readiness'` produces a look the rules reject

Suppose you invent the entity. What is in the body? Readiness has no referent in the world. Nobody in Reykjavík has a readiness. It is SLATE's calibration wearing a Title Case word — the number 1.35 is the giveaway. So:

- Rule 10: "No formula is ever a level. Coefficients may appear inside a sentence; they may not be the sentence." Readiness *is* the sentence. Its seven `ways` are the seven terms, and each way's required `detail` (rule 7, "what is behind it") is that term's coefficient — 0.45–1.15 for energy, 1.12–0.62 for stress. The `detail` line is where the arithmetic gets laundered into prose, seven times.
- Rule 6 / the shape gate: prose first, and a body that is only a grid of `Stat`s is rejected. Strip the arithmetic and nothing remains but a restatement of the label.
- The floor rule: "a look that would bottom out in a formula, a field name or a record has gone wrong, and **the look is wrong, not the world**." Here the world is wrong. The design has exactly one slot for this case — `provenance`, "one line at the foot of a body… never a level, never openable." Readiness is a look whose *entire* content is its provenance. The design has a slot for a calibration footnote and no slot for a calibration subject.

### Failure 3 — the mandated "why" machinery is the wrong arithmetic and is currently dead

Rule 10 requires any look answering "why" to build factors with `buildFactors` and render through `redactForPlayer` (`src/engine/core/audit.ts:161`, `:138`). Both are unusable:

- `buildFactors` is **additive**: `contribution = weight * value`, `score = Σ contribution`, `weight = |w| / Σ|w|`. Readiness is a **product of seven ratios over 1.35**. Feeding it through `buildFactors` yields a `score` that is not 82 and per-factor weights that are not the contributions. The one sanctioned explanation engine cannot represent the one number that most needs explaining.
- `redactForPlayer(record: AuditRecord)` takes a *record*, not `buildFactors`' return value — they do not compose. And `sim.audit()` (`src/engine/core/simulation.ts:594`) has **zero callers** anywhere in `src/` (the only grep hit is the unrelated `sim.ledger.audit()` at `index.ts:456`). `universe.audits` is `[]` in every save. So the readiness look must fabricate an `AuditRecord` at render time, at which point every factor is `knowable: true` and `redactForPlayer` is a no-op ceremony.

### Failure 4 — the general break: `parent` is single-valued, the graph is not

This is the one that outlives readiness. The design's depth-2 example fixes `dial:person/stress`'s `parent` as the person. Readiness's ways lead to those same dials. So:

- Open Readiness → trail `You › Readiness`. Press "Energy" → energy's parent is the person, so rule 11 says you *crossed*, the pane opens, and `trailTo(energy)` renders `You › Energy`. **Readiness is deleted from the trail the instant you use it.** No crumb returns you. The claim "a push-stack cannot do this… arrives fully populated" inverts: the parent-derived trail erases the level you were standing in.
- The same dial row opens **in place** from the How You Are facet and **in a pane** from Readiness, because the container is computed from a field that encodes one of the two parents. Same word, same thing, two containers.
- Re-parenting the dials under readiness is worse: the nine dials stop hanging off the person and the design's own depth-2 example breaks.
- Underneath sits a flat contradiction: `useLook().path` is "materialised from `parent`, not from click history", while `open()` "pushes, or folds if `to` is already in the path". If `path = trailTo(leaf)` there is nothing to push onto and the cycle-fold rule is dead code; if `path` is click history, the "arrives at depth 4 fully populated" guarantee only holds for the tree-shaped part of a graph the mechanism itself calls a mesh.

### Failure 5 — `gone` is required and unreachable

Rule 4 makes `gone` mandatory. `readiness()` is total and clamps to `[5, 100]`; it is never absent while the person exists. Every derived figure inherits a required sentence that no crawl can reach and that `voice-check.mjs` will police anyway. The required-field discipline has no concept of a total function.

### Scope

This is not one number. Home has 21 `<Stat>`/`<Meter>` call sites and most are derived, not stored: `netWorth` (`finance.ts:27`), `weatherAt` (`weather.ts:168` — temperature is `meanC + halfRange * cos(2π(hour-15)/24)`, never stored anywhere), `place.sun` daylight, the six-day forecast, `wellbeingSummary`. The design's own boast is "roughly forty inert numbers become drillable in one edit"; the majority of those forty are calls, not fields.

### Smallest repair

**A computed figure is not a subject. It is a facet of the object it is computed from, and its terms are that facet's ways.**

- `Readiness` on Home gets `look={at('person', p.id)}` with the How You Are facet selected. Pressing the word still opens where it stands; the trail reads `You › How You Are`; the floor rule holds because you land on a person; the DAG problem evaporates because the dials' single `parent` genuinely *is* the person; and the 1.35 stays a `provenance` line where the design already put it.
- The one code change this needs is that rule 8 must soften from "a facet is never addressable as a subject" to "a facet is not a subject but is deep-linkable": `Subject` gains `facet?: string`, used only to preselect a tab, never entering the trail, the name, or `subjectKey`'s identity for cycle-folding. That is about three lines in `subject.ts` and one in `LookHost`.

Independently, and required either way: `parent` cannot carry both "where this hangs" and "how you got here". Seed `path` from `trailTo` on cold entry only, and let traversal append the edge actually walked — otherwise every cross-edge in the graph silently rewrites the player's history.

## 1. The hard case, walked. It ends in two presses, not five.

**The Land.** `HOLDINGS` (`src/engine/content/estate.ts:83-104`) is three things: The House, The Studio Lot, Company Headquarters. Check the save:

The design's defence ("a thing that cannot be looked at is not painted as though it can") is exactly backwards here: rule 3 makes "The Studio Lot" typographically identical to a preposition, so the only inference available is *this is not a thing in the world* — about the two things the premise is entirely about. That is an immersion break of precisely the kind the feature exists to prevent.

**The House.** `features: []`, `structureIds: []`, `marketValue: 0`. `Structure` and `Room` exist in the model and none are ever created, so there are no rooms to open. What is left is bedrooms 6, bathrooms 4, 5,400 sqft, built 1974 — a `Stat` grid, which is the record view rule 6 exists to ban, and which passes rule 6's gate by having one sentence written above it. It also prints `tenure: 'owned'` (`index.ts:149`) while `estate.ts:60` says *"There is no tenure, no mortgage, no landlord."* The floor of the chain is a record, and the record disagrees with the world.

**Condition.** `HOUSE.condition = 88`, and `estate.ts:64-67` says of the whole house shape: *"The shape of it is a placeholder... they are here, named, in one place, and they are somebody else's to set."* Exactly two true statements exist beneath it:

- it shifts sleep quality by `remap(property.condition, 0, 100, -0.12, 0.10)` (`life.ts:189`) — **a formula, which rule 10 forbids as a level**;
- it loses `0.012` a day, uniformly, for every property, forever (`life.ts:267`) — a formula with no inputs, one hardcoded constant, likewise forbidden.

And nothing raises it. The entire command surface of the game is `world.take_decision_action` and `world.mark_read` (`src/engine/world/world.ts:44,69`). There is no maintenance, no repair, no money leaving an account for the house. So the Condition look has **no legal `Way`, no legal `Act`, and no legal facet** — one sentence, at depth 4, under a trail four crumbs long, and nothing.

## 2. The real failure: every guard is edge-oriented, and this world is leaf-heavy

Read the eleven guards again. `tests/looks.test.ts` follows `ways[].to` transitively and asserts each edge resolves. **A look with `ways: []` has no edges and passes trivially.** The shape gate rejects >1 `.stat-grid` or a grid with no sentence above it — a body of one sentence and nothing else passes. `text-caps` and `ui-audit` assert nothing clips. `inventory --check` asserts a matrix line exists. The static scan checks kind spelling. Not one of them asserts that a look leads anywhere.

The design guarantees *every door opens onto something* and never guarantees *every room has a door out*. It was tuned on the Stress chain, which is the single densest subgraph in the repo (nine dials × traits × 813 attributes). Everywhere else the save is 1 person, 1 household, 3 accounts, 1 property. Leaf-heaviness is the dominant failure mode of this feature in this codebase, and it is the one thing unmeasured.

## 3. The flagship chain's own terminus breaks rule 10

Depth 1 enumerates the nine dials. `freshWellbeing()` (`life.ts:36-40`) confirms them: energy, stress, sleepDebt, morale, condition, fitness, travelFatigue, nourishment, hygiene. **Sleep quality is not among them.** `sleepQuality(sim, person)` (`life.ts:184-199`) is a pure function of five inputs, computed at the moment of sleep and never stored. Depth 5 — `dial:person_000001/sleep-quality`, the level the design calls *"a real destination, not a manufactured one"* — is a formula wearing a dial's address, in a namespace whose other nine members are state the world moves.

So rule 10 is already dead in the worked example, or the flagship chain is four levels deep. Either way, the ruling that kills the Condition chain is one the design does not itself obey.

## 4. There is no back, and `parent` teleports you

`parent` is singular. The house has three honest parents: the estate, the city, and — as the thing `sleepQuality` reads — your sleep. Whichever is declared, arriving from another path silently rewrites the trail into ancestry you never walked. Combined with `open()`'s fold-not-push rule and no history: drill Stress → What Sheds It → the house you sleep in → Condition, press Escape four times, and you are standing on The Land, which you never opened, with the stress chain unreachable by any affordance. The design lists three exits (crumbs, the word you pressed, Escape) and all three walk the *declared* ancestry. The most-praised field produces the disorientation the feature was built to remove.

## 5. The container runs out of tints before the chain runs out of levels

`app.css:13-15` and `86-89`: there are exactly three surface tokens. The mechanism allows two in-place steps "and stopping" — undefined behaviour for the third. Rule 11: *"Below 900px every look expands in place."* So on a phone every chain nests past the spec, **including the five-level stress chain shipped as proof**. The Land chain hits it on desktop too, at level 3, because it is one object all the way down and never crosses.

## 6. Ship-blocker, provable from the repo's data: the name gate rejects real cities

Rule 5's gate: `name`/`kind` "must not contain the text of any registered kind." The design's own rejection example is `'Dial'` against kind `'dial'`, so the check must be case-insensitive. `src/engine/content/world-data.ts` contains **30 cities whose names contain "City"** — Mexico City, New York City, Quezon City, Ho Chi Minh City, Panama City, Oklahoma City, Guatemala City, Kuwait City, Vatican City, Belize City, Cebu City, Kyiv City, Minsk City, Basel-City, Benin City, Sadr City, New Taipei City among them. Every one fails the moment kind `'city'` is registered — and `<Open to={at('city', place.city.id)}>` is call site #2 in the design's own API section. The gate cannot tell a machine word from an English one, and this gazetteer is full of the collision.

The flagship chain breaks the load-bearing rule at its middle joint. Every "What Sheds It / What Would Start It" pair in the game will be the same shape, because that is what the engine's knobs are.

### 2. Depth 3's contents in the doc are factually wrong, and the true contents are a constant

The doc lists **Highly Strung**, **Sleeps Anywhere** and **Steadiness** as what's multiplying stress recovery. None of the three does:

- `highly_strung` systemMods are `{ stressGain: 1.35, sleepQuality: 0.88, moraleSwing: 1.25 }` (`personality-traits.ts:58-63`). No `stressRecovery`, no `recoveryRate`. It belongs under *What Would Start It*, so **the depth-3 → depth-4 edge in the worked example does not exist in the world.**
- `sleeps_anywhere` is `{ sleepQuality: 1.18, travelFatigue: 0.85, relationshipDecay: 1.12 }` (`:167`). Same.
- "Steadiness" is not a string anywhere in `src/`. It is the `emotionalStability` slider, labelled **Emotional Stability** (`CharacterCreation.tsx:76`), and at the default 50 its contribution is exactly 1.0.

What actually multiplies it: `modifierFor(person, 'recoveryRate')` reads `person.traits` — the **craft** sheet — and `bootstrap.ts:388-403` gives the player `traits: everyTrait()` with `prodigy: true`. `favourableOnly` then keeps `health_conscious` 1.35 and `resilient` 1.2 and discards `burnout_prone` 0.7. Recovery is **1.62 for every character in every save that will ever exist.** Depth 3's sentence, "You shed stress faster than most people do," is not a fact about Anna. It is a constant. Three levels of drilling arrive at a number with zero variance and two ways in that every player will see identically.

The provenance line is wrong too: the complete set of craft traits touching `recoveryRate` is those three, so exactly **one** is discarded, not four.

### 3. The subject of the flagship chain is dead within one night

Stress has exactly two sources in the whole build: `life.ts:63`, gated on `energy < 15`, and `COASTING_STRESS_FLOOR = 14` (`:243`) which only applies to unattended days. Against that, `applySleep` sheds `effective × 4.2` (`:216`). A normal 7.5-hour night at the quality this character gets (≈0.82) sheds **25.9 points**. Stress starts at 18.

So the honest depth-2 summary on day two, and every day after, is:

```
One Of Your Nine
Stress
Zero. Nothing in your life is putting any on you.

→ What Sheds It — the hourly recovery, and what's multiplying it.
→ What Would Start It — you'd have to be nearly unconscious first.
→ The Night Ahead — nothing to take off.
```

Five layers of depth over a number that is zero forever, because casting, jobs and shoots — the only things that ever added stress — were deleted. The doc picked this chain because "every figure was already there." Every figure is there and none of them moves.

### 4. Depth 4 promises knobs and delivers dead fields

The doc says the trait layer shows "every knob it moves — each of which is a way back into a dial." So an honest depth-4 body has to print "nothing in the game reads this yet" next to a third of its ways, or silently hide them, in which case the "the graph is readable without walking it" claim (rule 7) is false. Either choice is an inspector talking about its own schema.

### 5. Depth 5 is not a thing in the world

`sleep-quality` is not one of the nine. `Wellbeing` is `{energy, stress, sleepDebt, morale, condition, fitness, travelFatigue, nourishment, hygiene}` (`life.ts:37-40`). Sleep quality is `sleepQuality(sim, person)` (`:189-200`) — a function evaluated at the instant of sleeping. Giving it `kind: 'dial'` and the eyebrow "One Of Your Nine" prints a false statement, and the doc's own name gate cannot catch it because "Sleep Quality" is clean Title Case. Depth 5 is a formula wearing a dial's costume, which is rule 10 broken a second time, in the layer the doc calls "a real destination, not a manufactured one."

### 6. The structural hole: facets have no prose slot

Rule 6 — "A body that is only a grid of `Stat`s is a record view and is rejected" — and the shape gate that enforces it are both defined on `Looked.body`. But `Facet` is `{ id, label, body, ways? }`. **There is no `summary` on a facet.** The doc's depth 1 puts the nine dials in the How You Are facet, as rows. That grid is precisely the record view rule 6 rejects, and it ships through the facet, unpoliced, in the design's own first layer. Three of those nine rows can never move in this build — `fitness` only decays 0.18/day with nothing to raise it (`:277`, gym deleted), `travelFatigue` only falls (travel deleted), `hygiene` is floored at 82 every day (`:320`). The player's first press opens a table with three frozen cells.

## Judgement

It reads as an inspector. The prose is good — the doc can write SLATE's voice, and depth 2 is genuinely a sentence about a life. But the chain's shape is `object → number → the multiplication that produces the number → a term in the multiplication → another number`. Depths 3, 4 and 5 are the coefficient table with sentences wrapped round each row. Rule 10 says a formula is never a level; the only reason SLATE has five layers of depth available today is that formulas were made into levels. The rule and the flagship example contradict each other, and the example is what will get built.

The deeper cause: SLATE's current build has no *world* under the wellbeing numbers. In a build with shoots, a stress chain bottoms out at "the night shoot in Hafnarfjörður that ran to four" — a moment, which is what rule 10 demands the floor be. With casting and jobs deleted, the only thing under Stress is `life.ts:70`. The doc chose the one chain whose depth is entirely arithmetic and called it the case that proves prose-first.

## Smallest repair

**Move step 6.** Do not build the Stress chain. Build the chain whose floor is already a place, a person or a moment in *this* build: `entry` → the calendar entry → the day it sits on → the estate/city it happens at. `subjectForRef` (`calendar.ts:57`) already addresses it, `CalendarWorkspace.tsx:27` already has the frozen-snapshot bug the design wants to kill, and every level is a thing rather than a coefficient. It proves the same three claims — liveness by re-resolution, `parent`-derived trails, one entry opening the same way in three places — without needing a `flow` kind at all.

Then, concretely:

1. **Delete the `flow` kind.** If a number's explanation is a multiplication, it belongs in the dial's own sentence and its `provenance` line, which rule 10 already provides for. This removes depths 3 and 5 of the doomed chain and makes rule 10 enforceable instead of decorative.
2. **Add `summary: string` to `Facet` and extend the shape gate to facet bodies.** One field. Without it rule 6 has a hole exactly the width of the design's own depth 1.
3. **Add a liveness gate to `tests/looks.test.ts`:** for every `dial` kind, run the fresh save forward thirty days through `world.skip_to_event` and assert the value changes. Stress, Fitness, Travel Fatigue and Hygiene all fail it today. A dial nothing can move is not a thing to look at, and the guard costs ten lines.
4. **Fix the doc's depth-3 body before anyone builds from it** — it names three traits, none of which touches stress recovery, and undercounts the discarded traits by three.

domain.subject: The 17 dead entity types — declared in model.ts, imported by nothing, stored in nothing
domain.where: src/engine/domain/model.ts: Bill:233, StudioPlant:313, Structure:332, Room:345, Zone:361, VehicleConfiguration:374, VehicleKeeping:403, Vehicle:419, Costume:503, Order:543, Teeth:571, Training:583, Mark:612, Running:627, Company:680, Division:728, Employee:742
