primitives.subject: Modal — can it stack? Yes visually, no behaviourally. Escape collapses the whole chain.
primitives.today: Props are exactly {title: string, children, footer?, onClose, wide?}. It renders inline (no portal): `.overlay` (fixed, inset 0, z-index 200, flex, align-items:flex-start, padding 10vh) wrapping `.modal` (min(640px,100%), max-height 84vh, flex column, head/body/foot, body overflow-y:auto). Escape is a window keydown listener registered per instance; backdrop click closes; `.modal` stopPropagation guards it. A second Modal rendered inside the first's children DOES paint (nothing in the chain establishes a containing block for fixed) and its own backdrop click correctly closes only itself. But: (1) both instances hold a live window Escape listener, so one Escape closes every open modal at once — a depth-3 chain vanishes to the page; (2) both overlays sit at the same 10vh top offset with no offset, scale or inset, so the child lands exactly on the parent; (3) --overlay is rgba(6,7,9,0.82), so two stacked backdrops leave the parent 3.2% visible and three leave it 0.6% — the thing you drilled from goes black, which is the exact opposite of looking closer; (4) no focus trap, no focus restore, no autofocus, no inert/aria-hidden on what is behind, no body scroll lock — a wheel over the child overlay still scrolls the parent's `.modal-body` underneath it, because the child is a DOM descendant of that scroller.
primitives.shouldOpen: A stack owner rather than N independent dialogs: one component holding an array of levels, rendering only the top one through a portal, popping exactly one level per Escape and per backdrop click, restoring focus to the element that opened each level. Header needs to become a slot, not a `title: string` — a drill-down header carries an eyebrow (what kind of thing this is), the name, a chip or two, and a `‹ Back To [parent]` control; none of that fits a string. Add an `onBack` and a `level` so depth can be shown as a real inset/offset rather than a re-dim, and cap the backdrop at one dim for the whole stack.

primitives.subject: Modal is trapped by an ancestor stacking context — the three TimeControls dialogs render inside `.topbar`
primitives.today: No createPortal anywhere in src. Modal renders where it is called. `.topbar` sets position:relative + z-index:20, which establishes a stacking context, so the Sleep, Skip To Event and 'You Would Miss Something' overlays cannot paint above z-index 20 no matter that they declare 200. Below 900px the rail drawer is position:fixed z-index:30 with a z-index:29 shade: open the drawer, press Sleep, and the dialog renders underneath the drawer and its shade. It happens to work everywhere else only because nothing else on the path is positioned with a z-index.
primitives.shouldOpen: Every overlay layer goes through one portal into a single root-level layer host, so where in the tree an object is drilled from can never decide whether the drill-down is visible. This is a precondition for the rule 'every object opens' — objects will be opened from the topbar clock, from the rail, from inside a menu, from inside another overlay.

primitives.subject: Modal has no route, no history and no persistence — a drill-down chain is invisible to the app's only depth machinery
primitives.today: `route` and `breadcrumbs` are React state (react-router-dom is a dependency but is imported nowhere in src; there is no URL, no History API, no refresh survival). `breadcrumbs` is the only thing in the codebase that models depth, it is capped at 6 (`.slice(-6)`), and revisiting a route truncates back to it. Every modal is instead local useState in whichever component opened it (CalendarWorkspace `detail`, TimeControls `sleepOpen`/`skipOpen`/`confirm`, SaveSlots `confirmDelete`). Worse, the global hotkeys 'h' and 'c' fire while a modal is open — they only skip INPUT/TEXTAREA/SELECT — so pressing h behind an open Sleep dialog changes the screen underneath it while the dialog stays.
primitives.shouldOpen: One drill stack that the breadcrumb trail reads from, so 'Estate › South Field › The Barn › Roof' is one continuous path whether a step was a screen or an overlay, and one keyboard model where the stack consumes Escape/Backspace and swallows global hotkeys while it is deep.

primitives.subject: Panel — the container, and today the only shape a section of world can take
primitives.today: `.card` + optional `.panel-head` with title/subtitle/actions slots. `flush` kills padding for edge-to-edge lists, `tight` drops 24px to 16px. It has no onClick, no href, no `open`: a Panel is never itself a way in — only its `actions` slot is. Nesting a Panel in a Panel gives you --surface on --surface with a 1px --line border and 48px of doubled padding, so an inner level reads flat, not deeper.
primitives.shouldOpen: The panel header should be able to say what the panel is *of* (an eyebrow naming the parent object) and offer an Open. The token ramp for depth already exists — --surface / --surface-2 / --surface-3 / --surface-hover — but no component uses it as depth; `.callout`, `.holding` and `.trait` all sit at --surface-2, which is the 'one level inside a card' shape waiting to be formalised.

primitives.subject: Stat — the atom of information, and the highest-value drill target in the game
primitives.today: `{label: string, value: ReactNode, note?: ReactNode, tone?}`. Pure presentation: no onClick, no hover state, no focus state, no cursor change. Home alone renders ~20 of them (Cost Of Living, Income Tax, Industry, Daylight, Currency, Net Worth, Household). value being ReactNode means you *can* hand-wrap a `button.link` inside it — that class exists (app.css:328, 'a name that is also a way in') and is used nowhere.
primitives.shouldOpen: Every one of those numbers has a derivation the engine already computed and threw away — Cost Of Living opens into its basket, Income Tax into the bracket table from content/tax.ts, Daylight into the sun model, Net Worth into the ledger's accounts and the asset list. Stat needs an optional `onOpen` plus a hover/focus affordance, and `label` needs to widen from string to ReactNode so the label can carry the source. This single change makes roughly a hundred existing numbers drillable.

primitives.subject: Meter — a number with a bar, and the one primitive with no way in at all
primitives.today: `{label, value, max, tone, hint, invert}` — all scalars, no children, no ReactNode slot, no click. role="meter" with correct aria. Derives its own tone from percentage. Used for Energy, Stress, Readiness, Public Fame, Professional Reputation, Industry Demand, and the estate's Condition.
primitives.shouldOpen: A meter is a claim about state and every one of these has contributing terms the engine holds (life.ts readiness, reputation components, HOUSE.condition). Opening one should show what pushed it there, the last few changes, and what would move it. Needs an `onOpen` and a children/detail slot; today you cannot even attach a footnote without wrapping it externally.

primitives.subject: Empty — the only primitive that already invites a next step
primitives.today: `{title, body, action?: ReactNode}`. The `action` slot is free-form ReactNode, so it composes with anything. Used with no action in every current call site (CalendarWorkspace 143,173; WorkspaceRouter hand-rolls its own copy of the markup instead of using it).
primitives.shouldOpen: Nothing structural to fix. It is the correct shape already: an empty state that names what could be here and offers the way to make it exist. Worth using rather than re-writing `.empty` markup by hand (WorkspaceRouter.tsx:11-15 is a divergent copy).

primitives.subject: details/.sheet — the only true in-place disclosure, and it dead-ends one level down
primitives.today: `<details className="card sheet">` with a summary carrying a `.sheet-title` and a count chip, and a `.sheet-grid` (auto-fill 240px, max-height 460px, own scroller). Native: keyboard-operable, no JS, nests legitimately (details in details works). Two hard limits: the toggle word is baked into CSS as `content:'Show'`/`'Hide'` on `.sheet[open] > summary::after`, so it cannot say 'Open', 'Read The 412', or anything object-specific and cannot be translated or driven by state; and `.sheet-item` renders as plain divs, so a sheet of 400 attributes is a terminal leaf — you can open the list, you cannot open an item in it.
primitives.shouldOpen: This is the right primitive for level 2 of everything (a field's crops, a room's contents, a company's slate) because it expands the world rather than covering it. Make the summary label a prop, make `.sheet-item` a button that hands the item to the drill stack, and allow a nested sheet inside a sheet with the surface stepping --surface-2 → --surface-3 so depth is visible.

primitives.subject: .list-item — the row that opens. The closest thing to a drill-down primitive that exists.
primitives.where: src/styles/app.css:435-459; used at CalendarWorkspace.tsx:147,177, TimeControls.tsx:193, Home.tsx:181
primitives.today: Styled to be a `<button>` (transparent, no border, text-align left, width 100%, cursor pointer) with `:hover` → --surface-2, a `[aria-selected="true"]` → --accent-dim state, a bottom hairline, and careful wrap behaviour (flex-wrap, `.grow` floors at 14rem, full-width below 560px). Used as a real button three times and as a static div once (`.list-static` kills the pointer and the hover). It has a *selected* state but no *openable* state: no chevron, no 'opens into' affordance, and nothing distinguishes a row that selects from a row that drills. There is no React component for it — every site hand-writes the markup, so the row anatomy (swatch, `.grow` with title+meta, trailing chips) is copy-pasted with drift.
primitives.shouldOpen: Promote it to a `Row` primitive with a required 'what happens when you press this' — select vs open — and a trailing affordance for the open case. It is already the correct shape for a list of any objects; it should be the shape a drill-down list always takes so the player learns one gesture.

primitives.subject: chip — a label that is sometimes a button, with no hover or pressed styling of its own
primitives.where: src/styles/app.css:351-374; CharacterCreation.tsx:551-568 (as button, aria-pressed) vs CalendarWorkspace.tsx:161-162,189-190 (as span)
primitives.today: `.chip` is inline-flex, flex:none, white-space:nowrap, pill, --surface-3, with tone variants (accent/positive/negative/warning/info; positive and info are defined and unused). There is no `.chip:hover`, no `.chip:focus` and no `[aria-pressed="true"]` rule — the creation screen has to pass inline styles to show a chip is on (CharacterCreation.tsx:556-559). `.chip-row` exists solely to pull back the 9px --chip-inset so chips line up under a label. Chips cannot nest anything: nowrap, flex:none, one line, by design.
primitives.shouldOpen: A chip is the natural 'this fact belongs to another object' marker — a Clash chip should open the thing it clashes with, a currency chip the currency, a genre chip the genre. Needs a real interactive variant with hover/focus/pressed in CSS instead of inline styles, and a rule that a chip either labels or opens, never both.

primitives.subject: Term — a tooltip primitive that exists, is exported, and is used nowhere
primitives.today: `<span className="tooltip-term" title={explain}>` — a dotted underline and cursor:help. Zero call sites. As built it cannot work for drill-down: a `title` on a non-focusable span is unreachable by keyboard, invisible on touch, cannot hold markup or a number, and cannot be a way in to anything.
primitives.shouldOpen: The 'glossary' layer of the rule — a term in prose that explains itself on hover and opens fully on press — is exactly this component done properly: focusable, a real popover (the `.menu` shape below is close), and an Open into the full entry. It is the cheapest way to make running prose obey the rule without turning every sentence into links.

primitives.subject: .menu / .menu-item — a working popover with a two-line item, used only for Advance
primitives.today: Anchored absolute to `.menu-anchor`, min-width 18rem, handles outside-mousedown and Escape locally, becomes viewport-pinned fixed below 620px. `.menu-item` is a two-line button: `.menu-item-label` plus `.menu-item-detail` — a name and what is behind it, which is precisely the 'peek before you commit' shape drill-down needs. Not portalled, so anywhere inside `.main` (overflow-y:auto) it will be clipped or scroll away from its anchor; its own Escape handler will fire simultaneously with any Modal's.
primitives.shouldOpen: This is the right shape for level 1 of a drill — press an object, get a small card naming it with three or four ways in, each with a line of detail. It needs the same portal + single-Escape-owner treatment as Modal before it can be used away from the topbar.

primitives.subject: .picker-results / .picker-option — the narrow-a-huge-set primitive, stranded in character creation
primitives.today: A bordered scroller (max-height 340px) of two-line options (`.picker-option-name` + `.picker-option-meta`) with role=listbox/option, `[data-selected]` and hover/focus states. LocationPicker around it is the best existing model of progressive narrowing in the repo: map or country → region → search → 60 visible matches with a count of the remainder, lazily loading one country's data at a time.
primitives.shouldOpen: Nothing about this is creation-specific. Any drill into a large set — people, titles, parcels of the 2,000 acres, ledger entries — wants exactly this: pick a coarse bucket, narrow, search, cap the render and say how many more there are. It should move out of ui/creation into components as the standard 'choose from many' layer of the stack.

primitives.subject: .tabs / .tab — a facet primitive fully styled in CSS with no component and no call site
primitives.today: Scrollable tab strip with `[aria-selected="true"]` → accent underline. Defined, never rendered anywhere in src.
primitives.shouldOpen: Drill-down needs a lateral move as well as a downward one: once an object is open, its facets (Condition, People, Money, History) are tabs inside that level, not four more levels. This is free — the CSS is written; it needs a component and a rule for when a facet is a tab versus when it is a new level.

primitives.subject: .scene and .scene-choice* — a fully styled 'the thing in front of you' card, orphaned by the deletions
primitives.today: `.scene` is a card with a 3px accent left edge, a `.scene-min` compact form, a `.scene-interrupted` warning form, and choice states (`.is-primary`, `.is-danger`, `.is-hinted`, `.is-disabled`) plus `.scene-transcript li.is-you`. Every one of these is unused — the scene system was deleted, the CSS survived.
primitives.shouldOpen: This is a ready-made visual grammar for 'the object you are looking at right now, distinct from the panels around it', and its choice states are a ready-made grammar for the ways in and out of it. Either adopt it as the header shape of a drill level or delete it; leaving it is a trap for whoever builds this next.

primitives.subject: .dest / .dest-grid — the tile grid of ways-in, orphaned when Where To left Home
primitives.today: auto-fill 210px grid of tiles, each a label plus a `.dest-detail` line about what is behind it, with hover and an `.is-locked` state that dims rather than hides. Unused: Home no longer renders a destination grid and the rail took over. destinations.ts still models `locked` with an honest 'Under Construction' toast (GameShell.tsx:46).
primitives.shouldOpen: The 'ways in from here' surface every drill level will need — an object opens, and the tiles are the places it leads. The locked pattern in particular is already the house answer to 'this exists in the world but is not built', which a rule that promises every object opens will need constantly.

primitives.subject: .master-detail — a phantom class: named in the containment rule, never defined
primitives.today: The only rule mentioning it is `.master-detail > *, .side-by-side > * { min-width: 0 }`. There is no grid, no columns, no responsive behaviour — the layout was deleted and the min-width guard survived. Using `.master-detail` today silently gives you a plain block. Its sibling `.side-by-side` IS fully defined (minmax(240px,1fr) + 220–320px sidebar, collapsing at 700px) and is used nowhere.
primitives.shouldOpen: Master-detail is the other half of drill-down: a list on the left, the opened object on the right, one level deep without an overlay at all. Either rebuild it properly or delete the dangling selector — and `.side-by-side` is a working two-thirds of it, already responsive.

primitives.subject: SaveSlots re-implements the modal by hand instead of using the primitive
primitives.today: Hand-written `.overlay` > `.modal` > `.modal-head`/`.modal-body`/`.modal-foot` with its own role/aria-modal/stopPropagation. It has no Escape key handler at all, unlike the real Modal.
primitives.shouldOpen: Not a drill-down surface itself, but it is the proof that the primitive is easy to bypass: the moment a fifth call site needs a header the `title: string` prop cannot express, someone hand-rolls the markup and the stack loses that level. Whatever the drill stack becomes has to be the only way to open a layer.

primitives.subject: .hint has no base rule — a whole class of secondary explanation renders as plain body text
primitives.today:
`.hint` appears in the containment word-break list and in two descendant overrides (`.worldmap-empty .hint`, `.portrait-controls .hint`), but there is no `.hint { }` declaring size or colour. Every `

` outside those two contexts renders at full body size and full text colour, competing with the content it is annotating.
primitives.shouldOpen: Drill-down lives or dies on the tier below the fact — the line that says where a number came from. That tier needs a real, defined style (`.hint` or a renamed `.provenance`), because it will appear on every level of every stack.

primitives.subject: .gap-3 and .is-fixed — class names used in TSX that no CSS rule defines
primitives.today: `.gap-3` is undefined; `.col` happens to default to gap:var(--s3) so it looks right by accident and would break the moment `.col`'s default changed. `.is-fixed` is undefined, so a non-interactive `<div className="trait is-fixed">` inherits `.trait`'s `cursor:pointer` and hover border — three cards on the Career step look pressable and do nothing.
primitives.shouldOpen: The second one matters for the rule directly: if everything is going to open, then the boundary between what opens and what does not must be visible and honest. An affordance that lies is worse under this rule than under the current one.

systems.subject: Energy meter
systems.today: Inert. Meter renders a div with role="meter" and no click target (primitives.tsx:59-89). The number is a stored field, player.wellbeing.energy, with no explanation anywhere.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: the two writes that produce it — applySleep put back `effective × 13.5 × banked × energyRecovery`, applyElapsedWellbeing took `3.0/hr × hours × (1 + sleepDebt/24 × 0.5)`. L2: each multiplicand named — ENERGY_DRAIN_PER_HOUR (life.ts:27), the sleep-debt penalty, and the coasting ceiling of 74 that capped it if the night was unattended (life.ts:242, 313). L3: `banked` → recoveryFactorAt(age) (lifespan.ts:68) and `energyRecovery` → dispositionOf (taste.ts:139). L4: recoveryFactorAt sums the AGING band table year by year (lifespan.ts:43-52, each band carries its own sentence); dispositionOf splits into the named personality traits held (Early Riser 1.1, Homebody 1.15, Night Owl 0.94, Restless 0.9, Burns Out 0.9) × the conscientiousness lean (taste.ts:126).

systems.subject: Stress meter
systems.today: Inert number. Nothing says why it is 18 rather than 40, and nothing distinguishes stress that was gained from stress that failed to shed.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: the two flows — gain only fires below 15 energy (`hours × 1.6 × traitDrain`), shed always runs (`hours × 0.35 × recovery`), sleep sheds `effective × 4.2`, and an unattended night refuses to go below the coasting floor of 14. L2: traitDrain = modifierFor('stressPerShootDay') × dispositionOf('stressGain'); recovery = modifierFor('recoveryRate') × dispositionOf('stressRecovery'). L3: dispositionOf = traitModifier × axisModifier, so the panel can name the four or fewer personality traits actually contributing (19 of the 35 personality traits carry stressGain) alongside the emotional-stability and ambition leans (taste.ts:124-125). L4: modifierFor runs favourableOnly because the player is a prodigy (attributes.ts:1345), so the honest layer names the craft-trait multipliers that were *discarded* rather than pretending they did not exist.

systems.subject: Readiness
systems.today: A single 0-100 number with a hint sentence. The best drill-down target in the build and the most opaque thing on the screen.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: it is already a product of seven named factors, each a remap with stated endpoints — energy (0.45→1.15), stress (1.12→0.62), sleepDebt over 0-30 (1.05→0.66), nourishment (0.78→1.05), morale (0.82→1.12), travelFatigue (1.00→0.80), hygiene (0.92→1.03), all divided by 1.35. Rank them by distance from 1.0 and you have a factor list with no new maths. L2: five of those seven inputs — sleepDebt, nourishment, morale, travelFatigue, hygiene — are simulated every day and displayed on no screen in the game. Opening Readiness is the only way a player would ever learn they exist. L3: each of those five has its own chain back into applyElapsedWellbeing / applySleep. L4: and from there into age ceilings and disposition.

systems.subject: "Holding up." — the wellbeing sentence
systems.today: A flat sentence. The player cannot tell which condition produced it or how close the next one is.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: it is a seven-rung priority ladder with hard thresholds — energy <15, sleepDebt >20, stress >78, nourishment <25, the good case (energy >75 and stress <30), morale <30, else 'Holding up.' The drill says which rung fired and, more usefully, which rung you are nearest to and by how much. L2: each threshold's own field, opening into that field's chain.

systems.subject: Sleep quality (invisible input)
systems.today: Never displayed. It is returned by the life.sleep command result and consumed silently, yet it is the largest single lever on the energy the player does see.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: base 0.72, plus the house condition remapped to −0.12..+0.10, minus stress remapped to 0..0.24, plus recoveryRate trait ×0.06−0.06, all multiplied by dispositionOf('sleepQuality'), minus 0.08 for a 1am-5am bedtime, clamped to 0.28..1. Every term is a sentence. L2: the house-condition term links straight to The Land panel's Condition meter — the one place in the build where two displayed numbers are already causally wired together and nothing says so. L3: the trait layer (Light Sleeper 0.8, Sleeps Anywhere 1.18, Highly Strung 0.88, Indulgent 0.92) and the conscientiousness lean.

systems.subject: Condition meter (the house)
systems.today: Shows snapshot.home.condition, seeded at 88 by HOUSE (estate.ts:105). Inert, and nothing on the screen says what it is for.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: it wears at exactly −0.012 per local day, applied in dailyRollover to every unsold property, with no repair, no maintenance and no spend existing anywhere in the build — so the honest first layer is 'falling, slowly, and nothing can currently stop it.' L2: what it feeds — the property-condition term inside sleepQuality, and through that, energy. L3: HOUSE, its bedrooms, its 5,400 sq ft, its 1974 build year and the 2,000 acres it stands on, all in estate.ts. Note the naming collision: person.wellbeing.condition is a completely different number, is moved by nourishment, stress and sleep against a hard age ceiling, and is displayed nowhere.

systems.subject: Net Worth
systems.today: One compact figure plus a note reading '$0.00 in assets' — which is permanently true, because the assets loop needs property.ownerId to match, and the house is created with ownerKind 'none', no ownerId at all, and marketValue 0 (src/engine/index.ts:139-163).
systems.shouldOpen: L1: cash + assets − liabilities, with the assets branch honestly reported as empty and why (the land is the family's, not the character's — which is the premise, not a bug). L2: cash broken into the accounts that make it, liabilities into the accounts that owe. L3: each account balance decomposed into the postings that produced it — the ledger's stated LAW is that a balance is never a number someone typed (ledger.ts:1-8). L4: each posting's LedgerTransaction, which already carries memo, category, at, refType and refId — a pointer back at the thing in the world that caused it. This is a four-layer chain that exists in data today and is surfaced nowhere.

systems.subject: Everyday Checking balance
systems.today: A figure. No statement, no history, no way to ask what moved it.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: the account record itself — institution, last4, openedAt, kind, and for a card the creditLimit and the 22.49% APR. L2: its postings in time order. L3: the single opening transaction that seeded it from WEALTH_PROFILE[config.wealth] (bootstrap.ts:196-203), whose note string ('Getting by, with a card you're carrying a balance on') is written and only shown on the creation screen. L4: the creation choice that picked that profile.

systems.subject: Public Fame / Professional Reputation / Industry Demand
systems.today: Three meters that have never moved and cannot move. seedReputation writes them once at creation and no system in the surviving build ever writes reputation again — grep confirms bootstrap is the only writer.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: the truth, in the style doc's own terms — 'this is where you started; nothing has moved it yet.' publicFame = round(stage² × 42), professionalReputation = round(stage × 46), industryDemand = round(stage × 38), where stage is the career-stage slider ÷ 100. The squaring on fame is a design statement worth showing: fame is superlinear in how established you already are. L2: the four seeded siblings that are not displayed — audienceAppeal 50, reliability 55 + conscientiousness × 0.2, prestige stage² × 30, controversy 0. L3: what would move each once the industry exists, which is where the drill-down becomes a promise rather than a report.

systems.subject: Cost Of Living index, and the rent note under it
systems.today: An integer and a monthly rent in krónur. Reads like a looked-up fact. It is not: Reykjavík is not one of the 44 calibrated cities, so both numbers are derived.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: base = COUNTRY_PRICE_LEVEL['is'] = 145 (US = 100), then scaled by a population curve, scale = log10(pop) − 3, index = round(base × (1 + scale × 0.13)). L2: rent = round(index × 16.5 × (1 + scale × 0.22)); home price = rent × 320 — so all three figures are one figure. L3: the provenance already written onto the record — source 'calibrated_estimate', confidence 'low', and a note string that says in full sentences that the cost figures are derived from country and population, not looked up. L4: the ISK conversion (RATES['ISK'] = 138) and RATES_NOTE. Every layer here already exists as data; none of it is rendered.

systems.subject: Income Tax — "20% · Effective on $60,000"
systems.today: One rounded percent. place.ts computes the full TaxComputation and then keeps only lines.reduce(sum) ÷ 6,000,000. The richest ready-made drill-down in the codebase, thrown away at the last step.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: the four buckets computeAnnualTax already returns separately — federal, regional, local, payroll — plus net. L2: lines[], where every layer already carries a label, an amount and a hand-written note sentence ('Progressive brackets on $52,150 after deductions'), and the payroll line names its own wage base cap. L3: the IncomeTaxRule behind each line — its brackets, its standard deduction, its flat rate, its effectiveFrom/To. L4: resolveIncomeTaxLayers walking the jurisdiction path country → region → city, which is why the same income is taxed differently three streets away. L5: that the reference income is $60,000 and is TAX_REFERENCE_INCOME (place.ts:46), not the player's own — a caveat the note half-states and a drill-down should state fully.

systems.subject: Sales Tax / Property Tax
systems.today: Two percentages on one line, the second squeezed into the note. No indication that either is category- or date-sensitive.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: which rule was selected and at what jurisdiction depth — resolveRule (tax.ts:310) picks the most specific rule effective at sim.now. L2: the rule's category exemptions (the call passes 'general'; groceries and other categories resolve differently). L3: its effectiveFrom/effectiveTo, i.e. that a tax rate is a thing with a date. L4: the contradiction worth surfacing — the house's own annualPropertyTaxRate is 0 (index.ts:159) and nothing in the build charges property tax, so the displayed rate is about the place, not about the player.

systems.subject: Industry — "0/100"
systems.today: A zero with the note 'Film and Television work here'. The single most thematically loaded number on the screen and the least explained.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: it is zero because deriveCity hardcodes industryPresence to 0 for every city outside the 44 hand-calibrated ones — the industry is where SLATE says it is, and nowhere else. L2: the comparison that makes it mean something — Los Angeles 100, Burbank 96, New York 88, Vancouver 82, Atlanta 78, and Reykjavík 0. L3: ESTATE_NOTE (estate.ts:113) is written about precisely this number and appears on no screen: there is no business here to join, and that is the point of the save. L4: the lot and the company standing on the land against that zero.

systems.subject: Daylight — sunrise, sunset, "4h 21m of light"
systems.today: Two times and a duration. Reads as a lookup. It is real NOAA solar geometry computed from scratch, and at 64°N it is the most dramatic number in the game across a year.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: the four astronomical quantities the function already names — day of year, the fractional-year angle, the equation of time, the solar declination — then the hour angle that latitude and declination together allow. L2: why this latitude in particular: |cos(hour angle)| > 1 means the sun does not clear the horizon at all, which is the polar day / polar night branch the code already returns and Home already prints. L3: the same calculation on any other day, which turns the panel into a year curve. L4: that Reykjavík's swing is the reason the family land is where it is. This is the most immersive drill in the build: looking closer at the sky returns the sky's own reasons, with no game-system vocabulary anywhere in the chain.

systems.subject: Temperature now, and Humidity / Wind
systems.today: A big number, a condition word, and a line of humidity and wind. Feels like a forecast service; the panel's footnote already half-apologises for not being one.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: the hour curve — temperature = day mean + half-range × cos(2π(hour − 15)/24), coldest before dawn, warmest at three. L2: the day — normalFor(city, month, day) gives the climate normal, then three noise draws from sim.rng('weather', cityId, day) are blended 0.6/0.3/0.1 with yesterday's and the day-before's, which is literally why a cold snap lasts. L3: anomalyC — already computed, already rounded to a tenth, carried on every DayWeather, and displayed nowhere: 'today is 3.4 °C above normal for the date' is a sentence the data already knows. L4: the wet signal blended 0.65/0.35 against the climate's monthly wet-day chance, and what wet does (−1.5 °C, diurnal range squeezed to 0.6). L5: the climate profile and the latitude baselines under that.

systems.subject: The condition word — Clear, Fog, Overcast
systems.today: One word plus an emoji. No hint that it is a decision tree rather than a roll.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: the branch that fired, as a sentence — 'Fog, because this is an oceanic-profile coast, it is November, and the wind draw came in at 0.11, under the 0.18 fog threshold.' Every branch in that tree reads that way: Snow when wet and mean ≤ 0.5 °C; Thunderstorm when wet, high ≥ 24 °C, the climate is one of five, and the wind draw beats 0.55; Windy at ≥ 32 km/h; Overcast at cloud ≥ 0.65. L2: the cloud figure itself — profile cloud + 0.2 if yesterday was dry + a draw term. L3: the climate profile that set the thresholds.

systems.subject: Climate chip — "Subarctic"
systems.today: A chip in the panel header, terminal. It is the visible end of a five-layer resolution and looks like a label.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: how it resolved — city override, then region, then country, then a latitude fallback. Iceland resolves at the country level, so the answer is 'because it is Iceland', not 'because of where Reykjavík sits'. L2: the profile behind the word — tempOffset −3 °C, amplitude ×1.3, diurnal 8 °C, twelve monthly wet-day chances, a 30-day lag after the solstice, cloud 0.6. L3: the latitude baselines it modifies: mean = 28 − 0.0058·lat² − 0.05·lat, amplitude = 1.5 + 0.2·lat. L4: climateByLatitude, the fallback that would have applied — including its longitude test that tells a Novosibirsk winter from a Cork one. L5: the twelve other climate types, i.e. what everywhere else is.

systems.subject: The six-day forecast row
systems.today: Six tiles, each an emoji plus high/low, with the full condition in a title attribute only. Nothing opens.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: one day's whole DayWeather — DayWeather has 15 fields and the row renders 4. L2: that day's anomaly against the normal for that date. L3: why the run is correlated rather than six independent draws. L4: the same day next year or last year — weatherOn is pure in (seed, city, instant), so the panel can answer about any date the player asks about, forwards or back, at no cost and with no risk of a stale answer.

systems.subject: Local Time, zone abbreviation, hours from home
systems.today: A clock, a three-letter code, and a signed hour offset. Terminal.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: the offset is computed live — zoneOffsetMs(now, city zone) − zoneOffsetMs(now, home zone), rounded to the half hour, so it changes across a DST boundary and the drill can say so. L2: the IANA zone the city record carries, and whether summer time is currently in effect. L3: the city record's provenance — time zone and administrative parentage are public reference data, which the record already says.

systems.subject: Currency — "kr ISK · 138 per $1"
systems.today: Symbol, code, name, rate. RATES_NOTE already prints at the bottom of the panel, so the honesty is there but detached from the number it qualifies.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: the rate as SLATE's calibration, attached to the figure rather than a footnote three paragraphs down. L2: the writing rules the same table holds — symbol placement, decimal count (ISK shows none, KWD shows three). L3: the same sum written in this currency and in the ledger's, side by side, since the ledger is kept in one unit to the cent while the world is priced locally.

systems.subject: Country line — capital, continent, population, dialling code
systems.today: Four facts on one line. Nothing says which are public record and which are SLATE's, though every record already knows.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: the ReferenceRecord fields carried on every country, region and city and rendered on no screen — source, confidence, version, note (geography.ts:105-107, reference.ts). A country reads source 'public_reference', confidence 'high'; a derived city reads 'calibrated_estimate', confidence 'low', with a sentence explaining the derivation. L2: the region above it and the cities under it. L3: the languages, drives-on side, area — most of which Home already prints and none of which opens.

systems.subject: Next commitment, and "in 3 days"
systems.today: Title, relative time, absolute date, and a red warning when the player is in the wrong city. The best-behaved number on the screen and still a dead end.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: the ScheduledItem behind the entry (scheduler.ts:18-45) — kind, category, priority, durationMinutes, recurrence, createdAt, and refType/refId pointing at the thing in the world that booked it. L2: what jumping to it would cost, which skipTargets (calendar.ts:186-224) already computes in full and Home never calls: crossed commitments, which of those would be missed, whether travel is needed, and the note explaining it. L3: the conflicts entriesBetween already flags by real overlap, and the free windows freeWindows() already finds around them.

systems.subject: Decision urgency stripe and "Overdue"
systems.today: Urgency exists as a 0-100 number and is collapsed into three stripe colours. The due date shows; the reasoning and the life cycle do not.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: the sort that put this item at the top — overdue first, then urgency, then soonest due. L2: the item's own life cycle, which is a real rule set: past dueAt closes it silently, ninety days untouched dismisses it, a hundred and eighty days after closing deletes it from the save. L3: the actions' underlying commands and what each would execute (each action carries a commandKind and payload the player never sees named).

systems.subject: Household — "1 person"
systems.today: A count. Terminal, and currently always one.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: the Household record — memberIds, dependentIds, headIds, formedAt, residenceId, historyNotes (index.ts:69-79). L2: each member as a person. L3: the residence the household holds, which is the same property the Condition meter above it reports on — two panels describing one object with no link between them.

systems.subject: Calendar entry — Status, Length, Kind
systems.today: A modal with four Stats. The one place in the build where clicking a thing already opens a detail view — so it is the existing precedent the drill-down engine should generalise from, not replace.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: the conflict, when flagged — which other commitment, overlapping by how many minutes, both of which entriesBetween already identified pairwise. L2: the free windows around it that freeWindows() computes and nothing renders. L3: the ScheduledItem's refType/refId into the entity that booked it.

systems.subject: Holidays on a calendar day
systems.today: A name on a day cell. Terminal.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: the holiday in its own language and in English — holidayLabel already builds '元日 (New Year's Day)' and the entry carries both names. L2: whether it is national or regional, and which region code it belongs to (holidaysOn filters by regionCodeFor). L3: the same holiday across the year, or the country's whole year, which holidaysInYear already returns. L4: that holidays are loaded per country on demand, so the drill can honestly say when a country's file is not loaded rather than showing an empty day.

systems.subject: Season word in the greeting line
systems.today: One word beside the time zone.
systems.shouldOpen: L1: a month-to-season table, flipped below the equator by the city's latitude — genuinely one layer deep, and worth including in the sweep precisely because the drill-down engine needs a rule for numbers that bottom out immediately. Saying 'that is all there is to this one' honestly is better than manufacturing a second layer.

precedent.subject: Calendar day cell — the one drill-down still shipping
precedent.today: The whole cell is one <button>. Clicking it sets `selected` to the day key and a Panel of that day's entries appears far below the grid, with a Close button. Clicking the same day again toggles it shut. Nothing scrolls, so on a phone the reveal happens off-screen and the click looks like it did nothing.
precedent.shouldOpen: A day is a real object: the light (sun.ts already computes sunrise/sunset/daylight for the date), the weather model for that date, the country's observances, who else is committed that day, what the day costs you. Reveal-in-place is the right idiom; it needs to be anchored to the thing clicked rather than appended to the page.

precedent.subject: Calendar event pill inside a day cell
precedent.today: A lie. `.cal-event` sets `cursor: pointer` and each pill carries its own `title` tooltip, but the pills are <span>s nested inside the day <button> with no handler of their own. Clicking a named entry opens the day, not the entry. This is precisely the immersion break the feature exists to remove: the object announced itself as clickable and answered with something else.
precedent.shouldOpen: The entry itself — the same EntryDetail that the row below opens. A drill-down engine must make the smallest labelled thing the target, and must make it impossible to paint a pointer cursor on something with no destination.

precedent.subject: Calendar entry row → EntryDetail dialog (depth 2, terminal)
precedent.today: Works, and is the cleanest hand-rolled drill-down in the live tree: one `detail` state shared by two different lists, so the same object opens the same way from two places. The dialog shows four Stats and one sentence, then stops. Everything in it is a dead end: the Kind chip, the city name, the status, the length.
precedent.shouldOpen: Kind → the category and what the world does with it. City → the place. Status → why it is what it is. Length → what fills it. The dialog is the natural third layer and currently terminates the chain instead of continuing it.

precedent.subject: EntryDetail holds a detached snapshot of a live object
precedent.today: `CalendarEntry` is a projection rebuilt by `toEntry(item)` on every read; `setDetail(entry)` captures one and keeps it. The world clock runs at one world minute per real second while the dialog is open, so an entry that becomes `done`, `missed` or newly `conflicted` under the dialog still reads `Pending` until it is closed and reopened.
precedent.shouldOpen: Nothing — this is the bug the engine has to design out. A drilled layer must address its subject by identity (`{type,id}`) and re-derive from `sim` on every render, the way `useWorld` already does. VehiclesWorkspace got this right by passing `vehicleId` and re-reading; Calendar and Production Companies both passed the object.

precedent.subject: CalendarEntry.refType / refId — the entity pointer the engine already writes and nothing reads
precedent.today: Every calendar entry can already say what it is about — `refType: 'person'`, `refId: '…'` — and it is carried faithfully from the timeline item into the projection. No UI file in the tree reads either field. The pointer exists and dead-ends in the type.
precedent.shouldOpen: This is the seed of the engine's addressing scheme. `{refType, refId}` is already the same shape as `HistoryRecord.refs`, `DecisionItem.refType/refId`, `Notification.refType/refId` and the ledger's transaction refs. One resolver over that shape makes every one of those pointers openable at once.

precedent.subject: Production company card → dialog (the deleted precedent, and the best one)
precedent.where: git show 49df14f:src/ui/workspaces/ProductionCompaniesWorkspace.tsx:88 (the card is the button), :108-241 (the dialog)
precedent.today: Deleted at 5267cd4. It worked: the whole card was the <button>, the face carried one line each of the things that identify a company, and everything that made cards ragged moved inside. The commit that built it (9858dff) is explicit that the drill-down was the fix for a layout problem — 'fourteen names on a card is not a card, it is a wall'. That is the strongest argument in the repo's history for drill-down as a layout discipline, not just a feature.
precedent.shouldOpen: It stopped dead at depth 2. Nine labelled Blocks inside, every one of them terminal.

precedent.subject: The people inside the company dialog
precedent.today: Eleven named executives and casting heads rendered as `{name}` beside their role. Text. The named person was the deepest thing on the screen and the least openable.
precedent.shouldOpen: A person: what they run, what they have greenlit, whether they have ever met you, how you would get in front of them. The commit message for the whole section (ff2549a, '5267cd4 scrapped it') says casting was never built beyond the names carried in that data — the names were the stub of a system with no way to click into it.

precedent.subject: Chips in the company dialog: genres, cities, budgets, labels, known-for titles, agreements
precedent.today: Every chip is a real registry entity rendered as an inert <span>. `genresOf(studio)` returns genre objects; `citiesFor(studio)` returns gazetteer cities and the chip even reads '· you are here' when one matches where you stand — the code resolves the entity, proves it is the same city you are in, prints it, and offers no way in.
precedent.shouldOpen: A chip is the highest-density drill handle in the whole codebase and the most consistently wasted. If one rule ships first, it should be: a chip built from a registry object opens that object. `.chip-row` and `--chip-inset` were deliberately kept at 5267cd4, so the styling is still here.

precedent.subject: Parent Company printed as a Stat value
precedent.today: `<Stat label="Parent Company" value={studio.parent ?? 'None'} />` — the parent is another company in the same registry, eight of the eighteen had one, and it was a string. You could not walk from a label to its parent, and the comment beside it worries about the name being printed twice rather than about it being a door.
precedent.shouldOpen: The parent company, which opens the same dialog you are standing in, one level up. This is the cheapest possible proof that drill-down composes: same renderer, different subject, arbitrary depth.

precedent.subject: Bank account row → Statements, as a cross-tab filter
precedent.today: Deleted. A different and underrated shape: drilling did not open a dialog, it moved you to another tab *scoped to the thing you came from*, and the destination grew a button reading 'Every Account' to widen back out. It carried the id, not the object, so it stayed live.
precedent.shouldOpen: Nothing was wrong with it except that it was hand-wired once. A general engine should support 'open X in the context of Y' as a first-class move, with the un-scoping control generated rather than remembered.

precedent.subject: Relationships master-detail
precedent.today: Deleted. List on the left, detail on the right, `aria-selected` on the row, and `selected = circle.find(...) ?? circle[0]` so the pane is never empty. Drilling never covered the list you drilled from, which is the shape that best matches 'looking closer' rather than 'opening a window'. Inside the detail pane it went one further — Dates, Interactions — and then stopped.
precedent.shouldOpen: Third layer: an interaction, a date, a memory. The pattern supports it; the state (`selectedId`, `giftOpen`, `dateOpen` all flat siblings) does not.

precedent.subject: Vehicles modals take an id and re-read the world
precedent.today: Deleted. The only precedent that got liveness right: `<KeepingModal vehicleId={moving} />` and `<NameModal vehicleId={naming} />` take an id and look the vehicle up inside. Everything else in the repo — Calendar, Production Companies — passed the object and froze it.
precedent.shouldOpen: Nothing. This is the contract the engine should enforce for every layer: a layer is `{type, id}` plus a renderer, never a captured value.

precedent.subject: Instagram: five flat selection states, no stack
precedent.today: Deleted. The deepest hand-rolled drill-down SLATE ever had — feed → post → profile → thread → story — and it collapses under its own weight. `openWho = (id) => { setOpenId(null); setWhoId(id); }`: drilling from a post into the poster *closes the post*, so Back from the profile returns to the feed, not to the post you were reading. Every one of the 20+ `onBack` props is a hand-written guess at where you came from.
precedent.shouldOpen: This is the single clearest case for the engine being a stack rather than a set of booleans. Depth 3+ is not reachable by hand: five independent nullable states are 32 states, and the file only ever gets a handful of them right.

precedent.subject: The scene runtime — the real precedent for a sub-system you enter
precedent.today: Deleted at 62c30ca. Eighteen scenes, one runtime. A scene was a place you were *in*: it survived navigation ('mounted in the shell, above whatever screen you are on'), survived save and reload, carried a per-step `revision` so a stale or double click was refused, gave every commit an idempotency key, was place-bound so leaving the place interrupted it and returning resumed it, kept a transcript, and could be left with everything already done staying done.
precedent.shouldOpen: Nothing needs opening — this is the machinery the drill-down engine should be modelled on, one level up. A scene is a drill-down that commits; a drill-down is a scene that only reads. Registry + definition + persisted session + revision + survives-navigation is exactly the list a general engine needs, and it has already been written once in this repo and tested.

precedent.subject: Go Anywhere: entity search whose results throw the entity away
precedent.today: Deleted. It searched the actual universe — people, properties, vehicles, assets, every city, every airport, every car model, the whole catalog — and then every hit's `route` was a bare workspace route. Searching a person's name navigated to `/workspace/relationships`, which opened with `selectedId === null` and fell back to `circle[0]`. You found the thing and the game took you to the room it lives in and shut the door.
precedent.shouldOpen: The entity itself. This is the precedent that proves routes must be able to name an object. Everything needed to build the index already existed and worked; only the address was missing.

precedent.subject: 'Why Did This Happen?' — explanation as a drill-down
precedent.where: git show dc03b93:src/ui/workspaces/HistoryWorkspace.tsx:88-140; src/engine/core/audit.ts:21-60 (still in the tree today)
precedent.today: The screen is deleted; the engine behind it is not. `AuditRecord` still carries the question, the one-sentence answer, the weighted factors, the rules version, the seed, the roll, the probability and the score, with a `knowable` flag so information the character could not have is stored but never shown. The UI rendered it as a native <details> per record.
precedent.shouldOpen: Every number in the game. This is the deepest layer a drill-down can reach — not 'what is this' but 'why is it this' — and the data model for it is already written, already tested, and currently has no screen. `redactForPlayer` is the immersion guarantee: drilling can never surface what the character does not know.

precedent.subject: HistoryRecord.refs — 'for cross-linking from their pages'
precedent.where: src/engine/core/audit.ts:75-76; the only writer is src/engine/systems/life.ts:154
precedent.today: The field's own comment states its purpose: 'Entities this milestone concerns, for cross-linking from their pages.' Nothing has ever cross-linked. One system writes one ref (`{type:'person', id}`) and no reader exists.
precedent.shouldOpen: The person, the property, the project. Together with `CalendarEntry.refType/refId`, `DecisionItem`, `Notification` and the ledger's `refType/refId` on every transaction, there are five independent declarations of the same entity-pointer shape in the engine and zero resolvers.

precedent.subject: The Modal primitive cannot nest
precedent.today: No `createPortal`, so a Modal rendered inside another Modal's body is a DOM descendant of the outer `.overlay`, and a backdrop click bubbles to the outer `onClick={onClose}` and shuts both. The Escape handler is on `window`, so Escape also shuts both. `.overlay` is a single `z-index: 200` with no stacking. Every precedent avoided this by rendering modals as siblings at the workspace root — which is *why* every hand-rolled drill-down stopped at depth 2.
precedent.shouldOpen: The architecture, not a screen. Depth beyond 2 needs a portalled stack with per-layer focus trapping and an Escape that pops one layer.

precedent.subject: navigate() and breadcrumbs: routes name screens, never objects
precedent.today: `navigate(route, label)` pushes `{route, label}` and dedupes by route, so two different objects in the same workspace collapse to one crumb. Routes are literal strings in a `Record<string, () => JSX.Element>` (WorkspaceRouter.tsx:3-5). No parameters, no query, no entity. Meanwhile tests/navigation.test.ts:74 already does `route.split('?')[0]` — query strings are anticipated by the guard and produced by nothing.
precedent.shouldOpen: An addressable drill path. Breadcrumbs are the immersion-preserving affordance the shell already renders (GameShell.tsx:155-168) and they currently cannot describe a drill at all, because every drill lives in component-local state that dies on navigate and is absent from the save.

precedent.subject: Term — a 'look closer' primitive that is defined and never used
precedent.today: `<Term explain="…">` renders a dotted underline and a native `title`. Zero call sites in the entire tree. The dotted-underline style is still in the stylesheet. Meanwhile 25 places use a bare `title=` attribute as their only 'look closer' mechanism — invisible on touch, invisible to the walkthrough tool, and unstyleable.
precedent.shouldOpen: The shallowest rung of the ladder: a word in prose that opens what it means. If the engine has a real hover/press layer, `Term` is where it plugs in and `title=` stops being the fallback.

precedent.subject: Home — 'Where You Are': nine Stats, nine dead ends
precedent.today: Local time, daylight, currency with its per-dollar rate, cost of living with a local rent figure, income tax, sales tax, property tax, industry presence, languages, capital, continent, population, phone code, which side they drive on, units, film incentive. Every one is computed by `placeProfile` from real gazetteer data and every one is a terminal string. It is the densest surface in the game and the flattest.
precedent.shouldOpen: The country, the region, the city, the currency, the tax regime, the language, the climate. `src/engine/world/place.ts` already assembles all of it from linked registries — the links exist in the data and are severed at the render.

precedent.subject: Home — 'The Land'
precedent.today: The house name, 2,000 acres, a condition meter, a household count. Nothing opens. The estate content file defines `HOLDINGS` — the house, the studio lot, and the company headquarters — and Home does not render them at all.
precedent.shouldOpen: The estate is the premise and should be the deepest object in the game: land → the lot → the stages → the company → its slate. estate.ts's own header comment calls the third holding 'the whole game'.

precedent.subject: Creation — the three holdings on Starting Point
precedent.today: `HOLDINGS.map(...)` renders three plain <div>s with a bold label and a sentence. One of them is 'The Studio Lot' and one is 'Company Headquarters'. The card below names the company ([Surname] Pictures) and states that it 'has no record yet'. Three of the most important objects in the game, introduced to the player as static text, before the player has ever clicked anything.
precedent.shouldOpen: This is where the player first meets the drill-down rule, and where breaking it teaches them the world is flat. The lot opens onto stages; the company onto what it owns, who works there and what it has made; the house onto rooms.

precedent.subject: Creation — the Sheet disclosures
precedent.today: A native <details>: 'Every Acting Skill', 'Every Acting Trait', 'Mastery Of Every Genre', each with a count chip, expanding to a grid of name + one-line note. Expand-in-place, which is the right idiom and keeps context perfectly — and the fourth distinct drill-down shape in a codebase with only five screens left.
precedent.shouldOpen: Each item. A skill opens onto what it does, what raises it, where you stand on it. Currently the leaf is a 12px description string. Also worth noting: this is the third native-<details> precedent (HistoryWorkspace audits, ScenePanel transcript were the others) — expand-in-place is what SLATE reaches for when the drill must not cover the page.

precedent.subject: Decisions and notifications: an 'Open' button that can only name a room
precedent.today: Both `DecisionItem` and `Notification` carry `route?`, `refType?` and `refId?`. Home renders `<button onClick={() => navigate(decision.route!)}>Open</button>` — route only. The refs are dropped. A decision about a specific person opens the screen people live on, and the player has to find them again.
precedent.shouldOpen: The subject of the decision. The engine already knows it; the button already exists; only the address is missing. tests/navigation.test.ts guards that every route opens onto something — the same guard should be extended to every ref opening onto something.

precedent.subject: The walkthrough had to hardcode a click to photograph depth 2
precedent.today: To capture the company dialog the tool located `.studio` by the literal text 'NBCUniversal', clicked it, waited 800ms, shot it, pressed Escape. Every drillable surface needed its own hand-written click, and the section was deleted wholesale with the screen. tools/ui-audit.mjs measures every element at four widths but can only reach what is already on screen.
precedent.shouldOpen: A machine-enumerable drill graph. If layers are declared rather than hand-wired, the walkthrough can open every one of them, the audit can measure every one at four widths, and navigation.test.ts can assert that every declared drill target resolves — the same way it already asserts every engine route opens onto a screen.

immersion.subject: The breadcrumb trail, and labelForRoute behind it
immersion.today: Two crumbs at most — "Home › Calendar" — because ROUTE_LABELS has exactly two entries. Nothing deeper has ever been pushed.
immersion.shouldOpen: This is the single largest immersion hazard in the repo. navigate(route, label?) makes the label optional, and when it is omitted labelForRoute takes the last path segment, swaps - and _ for spaces and capitalises each word. Drill into Reykjavík with navigate('/place/is-39-reykjavik') and the trail reads "Home › Is 39 Reykjavik". Drill into a scheduled thing with its id (ids.ts:42-47 makes cal_0004f2) and it reads "Cal 0004f2". The estate ids in HOLDINGS are house/lot/company, so '/estate/lot' becomes the crumb "Lot". A trail that names slugs is a file path with a nicer separator. The fix is not a better slug-prettifier: the label must be the world's own name for the thing ("The Studio Lot", "Tuesday The 14th", "Stage Two"), passed explicitly and never derived, and labelForRoute should refuse rather than guess. Note the trail is also capped at six (game-context.tsx:167) and dedupes by route — a drill-down that revisits the same route with a different subject will silently collapse two different things into one crumb.

immersion.subject: "Where You Are" — the nine-Stat grid on Reykjavík
immersion.today: Nothing. It is not a control. But it is already the shape a naive drill-down would deepen into: nine label/value/note triples covering Local Time, Daylight, Currency, Cost Of Living, Income Tax, Sales Tax, Industry, Languages, and one whose label is the country name.
immersion.shouldOpen: A place you are standing in, not a longer table. Layer two is the city as a person in it experiences it — what the krona buys at the shop on the corner, how long the light lasts today and what that does to a shooting day, who else is here. Layer three is a specific street, a specific building, a specific person. The tell that this has gone wrong is that drilling produced more Stats. If layer two is 18 Stats instead of 9, the drill-down is a schema browser with a nice font.

immersion.subject: The Industry stat, printed as a fraction of its own scale
immersion.today: Renders `${place.industryPresence}/100` with the note "Film and Television work here". For Reykjavík that is 0/100.
immersion.shouldOpen: The "/100" is the anti-pattern in miniature: it tells the player they are looking at a field with a range, not at a fact about the world. Nobody standing in Iceland thinks "industry presence: zero out of one hundred", they think there is nobody to hire and no stage but the one the family just built. Layer two behind this should be the absence made concrete — no crews within a flight, no one who has done this here before, the specific reason ESTATE_NOTE (src/engine/content/estate.ts:112-116) gives in prose. Any drill-down that opens onto the number's provenance has opened the debugger.

immersion.subject: A Stat whose label is a data value (the country row)
immersion.today: Renders `<Stat label={place.countryName} value={place.capital || place.continent} />` — the label slot holds "Iceland", the value slot holds "Reykjavík", and the note concatenates continent, population and dialling code with middle dots.
immersion.shouldOpen: Nothing should open here as it stands. A label made of content is the visual grammar of a key-value dump: the player is reading a row of a record where the key happens to be a proper noun. Whatever depth Iceland deserves belongs behind the country's name as a name, not behind a stat cell that borrowed the label slot. This one line is the clearest existing example of the constraint's failure mode, and it is on the game's first screen.

immersion.subject: The Land — The House
immersion.where: src/ui/screens/Home.tsx:331-345; the record behind it at src/engine/content/estate.ts:70-77
immersion.today: Nothing clicks. A Stat reading "Home / The House / 2,000 acres, held by the family", a Condition meter at 88, and a Household count.
immersion.shouldOpen: This is the most tempting naive drill in the game and the worst one to get wrong. HOUSE is `{ name, bedrooms: 6, interiorSqft: 5_400, yearBuilt: 1974, condition: 88 }` and its own comment (estate.ts:64-69) calls the shape a placeholder the simulation needs. Open it naively and you get a property record: six bedrooms, 5,400 square feet, built 1974, condition 88. That is an estate agent's listing, which is exactly the old housing model the repo deliberately deleted. What should be behind it is rooms you can be in — the kitchen at seven in the morning, whose room is whose, what the 1974 roof does in an Icelandic January. Condition 88 should never be a number the player drills into; it should be the reason a room is cold.

immersion.subject: HOLDINGS — the three things standing on the land
immersion.where: src/engine/content/estate.ts:86-104; rendered as inert divs at src/ui/creation/CharacterCreation.tsx:863-870
immersion.today: Three non-interactive rows: The House, The Studio Lot, Company Headquarters, each with one line of prose. Nothing is clickable anywhere in the game.
immersion.shouldOpen: These are the first three drill targets the feature will ever have, and the estate is the one object in SLATE that genuinely goes five layers deep: estate → the lot → a stage → what is rigged in it → the specific piece of kit and who last used it. Two hazards are already in the data. First, each Holding carries `id: 'house' | 'lot' | 'company'`, which will end up in a route and then in a breadcrumb reading "Lot". Second, `label` is a function of lastName and `detail` is a single string — a two-field shape that can only ever render as a title and a caption. Depth needs the content model to carry more than a caption, or every layer will look like the layer above it with different words in the same two boxes.

immersion.subject: The calendar day cell
immersion.today: Clicking a day toggles a Panel below the grid listing that day's entries. It works. But the cell announces itself to a screen reader as `${formatDate(...)}, ${day.entries.length} entries` — "14 October 2027, 3 entries".
immersion.shouldOpen: "Entries" is the data-type word, and it is the word a blind player hears for every day of the game. Nobody has three entries on a Tuesday; they have three things on. The day itself has real depth — the day, then a thing on it, then the people at that thing, then one of those people — but every layer has to be named in the world's nouns. The same cell also drops overflow as "+2 more" (line 118), which is pagination language; "two more things" is the same width and is English.

immersion.subject: EntryDetail — the modal behind a calendar entry
immersion.today: Opens a Modal titled with the entry's own name (line 219 — correct, it names the thing not the type), containing a 2×2 grid of Stats: When, Length, Kind, Status, then one sentence of prose.
immersion.shouldOpen: The title is right and the body is a record view. Two specific leaks: `Stat label="Kind"` (line 223) is a data-type word in a label slot, and its fallback `titleCaseLabel(entry.category)` renders an enum id in Title Case, which is a raw id wearing a label's clothes. `Stat label="Status"` prints statusOf(entry), and statusOf only maps 'done'→'completed' — 'pending' and 'observance' reach the screen as the stored strings. Same chip at line 162. Behind an entry there is real depth: who else is on it, what it is for, what happens if you are not there. The prose at lines 231-237 is already reaching for that and is the best thing in the file; the Stat grid above it is the part that reads as a database row.

immersion.subject: The calendar legend, whose content lives in a title= tooltip
immersion.today: Five colour swatches with one-word labels. The actual writing — "Time that's yours.", "Birthdays of people you know." — is only in a title attribute, so it appears on hover, on a mouse, after a delay, and never on a phone.
immersion.shouldOpen: The hazard is structural rather than local: the codebase already treats `title=` as the place the next layer of detail goes. CalendarWorkspace alone uses it eight times (lines 94, 101, 112, 127 and others), Home four, and primitives exports a `Term` component (src/ui/components/primitives.tsx:154-156) whose entire body is a title attribute. If drill-down inherits that habit, the second layer of the whole game is a tooltip tree — undiscoverable, untouchable, and invisible to the text-caps and cohesion tools that check what is on screen. Depth has to be a place you go, not a thing that appears while you hover.

immersion.subject: The holiday mark — a glyph standing in for a word
immersion.today: A day with a holiday shows `✦`, with the holiday names only in its title attribute.
immersion.shouldOpen: docs/STYLE.md:74-87 forbids exactly this — "no Unicode glyph standing in for a word" — and the gate does not catch it, because tests/interface.test.ts matches Extended_Pictographic and ✦ is not pictographic. The same file uses ‹ and › for month navigation (lines 74, 76), primitives.tsx:144 uses ✕ to close a modal, and GameShell.tsx:161 uses › between breadcrumbs. Each is defensible alone; a drill-down multiplies them, because every new layer wants a chevron, a closer and an expander. A feature that adds ten layers under the current conventions adds thirty glyphs. Behind the mark itself there is a real second layer: the day as Iceland actually observes it, whose name in Icelandic the data already carries (holidayLabel, src/engine/content/holidays.ts:150-152).

immersion.subject: "How You Are" — the wellbeing meters, and Readiness in particular
immersion.where: src/ui/screens/Home.tsx:196-204; Meter at src/ui/components/primitives.tsx:59-92; readiness at src/engine/systems/life.ts:82-94
immersion.today: Nothing clicks. One line of prose from wellbeingSummary, then three meters. Meter always prints its number (primitives.tsx:75-78), so the screen says "Readiness 72".
immersion.shouldOpen: Readiness is a seven-factor product of energy, stress, sleep debt, nourishment, morale, travel fatigue and hygiene, normalised by 1.35 and clamped. Drill into the 72 naively and you get the factor breakdown, which is the game showing the player its own arithmetic — a stat sheet, not a world. wellbeingSummary (life.ts:96-105) is already the correct answer one layer up: "Badly short on sleep. Everything is harder than it should be." The deeper layer should keep going in that register — what specifically is wrong, since when, what would fix it — and the factor names (travelFatigue, sleepDebt) must never surface as labels. This panel is where the difference between looking closer at a person and opening their record is sharpest.

immersion.subject: The "Open" buttons on decisions and notifications
immersion.today: A decision or notification carrying a route gets a button labelled exactly "Open". It navigates and pushes a crumb.
immersion.shouldOpen: This is the "Details" button the constraint warns about, already shipped, twice. docs/STYLE.md:33-39 rules it out by name: a control says what pressing it does — Review Offer, Book Viewing — not OK, Submit, Go, Continue. "Open" is the same failure with a shorter word, and it is the label a drill-down will reach for at every single layer unless something forbids it. The comment on DecisionItem.route (src/engine/domain/model.ts:772-777) already worries about "an Open button onto nothing", which shows the button was noticed and kept. A decision knows what it is about; the button should say so.

immersion.subject: The Modal primitive
immersion.today: Takes `title: string`, renders it as an h2 and as the dialog's aria-label, plus a ✕ closer with aria-label "Close". Both current callers name a thing (the entry's title, "Sleep") rather than a type, which is right.
immersion.shouldOpen: This is the component every drill-down layer will pass through, so it is where the rule should be enforced rather than merely observed. Two structural gaps: the title is a bare string with no way to carry a subtitle that says what kind of thing this is without putting the type in the title, so a caller under pressure writes "Calendar Entry" or "Property Details"; and there is no notion of where you came from, so nested modals stack with no trail and no way back but Escape. Also worth naming: modals are the wrong container for depth past layer two — a modal over a modal reads as a dialog chain, and the world underneath stops existing.

immersion.subject: Money — the account panel
immersion.today: Three Stats: the primary account's name with its balance, Net Worth, and Owed. When there is no account the label reads "No account" — a sentence fragment sitting in a label slot where a proper noun goes.
immersion.shouldOpen: Money is genuinely four layers deep (net worth → an account → a statement period → one transaction → what was bought), and it is the system most likely to arrive as a ledger UI, because it already is one underneath. The immersion test here is whether layer three is a transaction list with amounts and dates, or the evening it describes. Also note RATES_NOTE (src/engine/content/currency.ts:28) and the climate note on Home.tsx:291-293 — the game tells the truth about being a model, which docs/STYLE.md:45-51 requires. Drill-down has to hold both: honest that a figure is SLATE's calibration, without the honesty turning into a model inspector.

immersion.subject: Standing — the three reputation meters
immersion.today: Public Fame, Professional Reputation and Industry Demand, each a meter with its number. Nothing clicks.
immersion.shouldOpen: For a character nobody has heard of, standing in a country with no industry, three numbers between 0 and 100 is the least true thing on the screen. Behind fame there are people who have or have not heard of you, and behind demand there is somebody who did or did not call. Layer two should be who, not how much. If drilling Public Fame opens a history chart of the number, the feature has become an analytics dashboard.

immersion.subject: The raw IANA time zone printed on the creation screen
immersion.today: A Stat labelled Time Zone showing the abbreviation as its value, with `{city.timeZone}` — the literal string "Atlantic/Reykjavik" — as its note.
immersion.shouldOpen: The clearest existing raw-id-on-screen violation, and it sits on a page the player reads before the game starts. docs/STYLE.md:109-116 requires a label map between an id and the screen, and that rule is about to be tested by a feature whose whole job is showing what is underneath things. The city id itself is 'is-39-reykjavik' (src/engine/content/estate.ts:24) and the entity ids are cal_0004f2 (src/engine/core/ids.ts:42-47); both are one careless key= or route away from the screen.

immersion.subject: WorkspaceRouter's empty state
immersion.today: An unknown route renders "Nothing Here Yet" over "That workspace doesn’t exist."
immersion.shouldOpen: "Workspace" is an interface word — it names the application's internal container, not anything in the world, and the player has never seen the term anywhere else. A drill-down multiplies dead ends by an order of magnitude, so this string will be read far more often than it is now, and every naive not-found message will name the type it failed to find ("no such entry", "that person doesn't exist"). The engine already does this in copy the player sees as a toast: 'No such decision.' (src/engine/world/world.ts:37, 47) and 'That action isn’t available on this item.' (line 49) — "decision" and "item" as record types, in the second person.

immersion.subject: The Sheet disclosure — the game's only existing expander
immersion.where: src/ui/creation/CharacterCreation.tsx:1050-1078; its Show/Hide labels injected from CSS at src/styles/app.css:562-569
immersion.today: A <details> that opens onto a scrolling grid of every skill, trait or genre — name and one-line note, 240px columns, max-height 460 with overflow-y: auto.
immersion.shouldOpen: Nothing deeper, and that is the point: this is the one legitimate reference table in the game, and its own comment defends it well ("a number that large is a claim rather than a fact until somebody can read it"). It is worth flagging because it is the shape that must not spread — if the drill-down feature reuses .sheet, every layer of the world becomes a scrollable card grid of name-plus-note. Two smaller things: the toggle words Show and Hide are generic verbs (docs/STYLE.md:33-39) and they live in a CSS `content:` string, where no gate can read them — label-sweep only scans src/engine/**/*.ts (tools/label-sweep.mjs:80) and voice-check only .ts/.tsx (tools/voice-check.mjs:35-37).
